factors.name: Exogenous ketones (ketone esters, ketone salts, MCT/C8 oil)

entries.headline: A ketone-ester drink raises blood BHB to ~2-4 mmol/L within an hour, and salts or C8 oil raise it much less. Acute doses lower glucose by ~0.5 mmol/L and give a small cognitive benefit, but they do not improve exercise performance, and the anti-inflammatory story is contradictory in humans.

dose.effective: Ketone monoester ~0.3-0.5 g/kg (about 12-27 g BHB) gives a peak BHB of ~2.8-4 mmol/L for 2-4 h. Ketone salts ~12-24 g BHB give ~1 mmol/L. C8 (tricaprylin) 20 mL twice daily gives ~0.3-0.5 mmol/L. A 15 g twice-daily MCT drink was used in the 6-month MCI trial.
dose.studied_range: Single doses up to 714 mg/kg monoester; 25 mL (26.8 g) monoester three times daily for 28 days in healthy adults; 12 g BHB before meals for 14 days in obesity; 30 g/day MCT for 6 months.
dose.too_much: Gut upset (nausea, cramps, diarrhoea) at high doses, worse with salts and MCT. Salts carry a large sodium/potassium load and half the BHB is the less useful L-isomer. Avoid with SGLT2 inhibitors or type 1 diabetes without medical advice.
dose.timeframe: Peak at 30-60 min, back to baseline within 3-4 h; no lasting ketosis without repeated dosing.
dose.notes: A meal cuts the peak by about a third. Ketone esters taste harsh and cost several dollars per serving at retail (a market observation, not from a study). They give ketones without carbohydrate restriction, so they do not reproduce the low-insulin, weight-loss and low-glucose milieu of the diet.

entries.mechanism: Supplies D-BHB directly. In the short term it lowers hepatic glucose output, free fatty acids and lipolysis (HCAR2), and gives the brain an alternative fuel. HDAC inhibition and NLRP3 blockade are cell and mouse findings. In humans, a single dose increased monocyte caspase-1 activation, while 14 days of pre-meal dosing decreased it.
entries.interactions: No human trials measure oxidative-damage markers. It does not replace [ketogenic-diet] for epilepsy. Glucose lowering adds to diabetes drugs. For athletes, pre-race ketone drinks impaired a time trial; post-session ester during overload training is the one positive signal.
entries.caveats: A meta-analysis of 13 RCTs found no performance effect (g = -0.05). The cognitive meta-analysis effect is small (SMD 0.29) across heterogeneous trials. Most trials are industry-linked, small and short. Vendor claims about 'burning fat' are backwards: exogenous BHB suppresses lipolysis.

key_numbers.label: Peak BHB, ketone salts (same BHB dose)

entries.title: Exogenous ketones (ketone esters, ketone salts, MCT/C8 oil)

entries.headline: Outside testosterone shuts down the brain's signal (LH/FSH) to the testes and can drop sperm counts to zero; recovery takes months to over a year.

dose.effective: Any exogenous testosterone or anabolic steroid, including gels, injections and 'cycles'.
dose.studied_range: Androgen regimens used for male contraception reliably suppress sperm output.
dose.too_much: Long-term, high-dose and long-acting preparations recover slowest.
dose.timeframe: Median recovery to 20 million/mL about 3.4 months after contraceptive-style androgen use; after steroid abuse, often 6-12+ months, sometimes incomplete.
dose.notes: AUA/ASRM: do not prescribe testosterone to men who want current or future fertility. Do not stop abruptly without medical advice; urologists can use hCG, SERMs or aromatase inhibitors to restart production.

entries.mechanism: Negative feedback suppresses GnRH, LH and FSH; intratesticular testosterone collapses, halting spermatogenesis (endocrine, not primarily oxidative).
entries.interactions: Overrides any benefit from diet or supplements. Often combined with other harmful exposures in body-building (high-dose supplements, stimulants).
entries.caveats: Not an SDF factor in the usual sense: it mainly lowers sperm number, often to azoospermia. Included because it is the most common avoidable cause of severe male-factor infertility in young men.
entries.title: Exogenous testosterone (TRT) and anabolic-androgenic steroids

entries.headline: In the 200-man EUROLIVE RCT, oxidized LDL fell linearly with olive-oil phenolic content at 25 mL/day; EU law authorises an LDL-protection claim for oils supplying 5 mg hydroxytyrosol and derivatives per 20 g, and PREDIMED's EVOO arm cut major CVD events by ~30%.

dose.effective: 20-25 g (about 2 tablespoons) per day of a high-phenolic EVOO meeting >= 5 mg hydroxytyrosol + derivatives per 20 g.
dose.studied_range: 25 mL/day for 3 weeks (EUROLIVE); ~1 L/week per household in PREDIMED for years.
dose.too_much: Calories (about 120 kcal per tablespoon).
dose.timeframe: Measurable LDL changes within 3 weeks.
dose.notes: Use as the main culinary fat, raw on food or for moderate-heat cooking; phenolics decline with storage, light and heat. Refined olive oil has a fraction of the phenolics.

entries.mechanism: Hydroxytyrosol and its secoiridoid precursors (oleacein/3,4-DHPEA-EDA, oleuropein aglycone) bind to LDL and protect its lipids from oxidation; high oleic acid content makes membranes and LDL less oxidizable than PUFA-rich oils; modest Nrf2 and anti-inflammatory effects.
entries.interactions: Best evidence when it replaces butter, refined seed oils or [oxidized-frying-oils]. Improves carotenoid absorption from [tomatoes-lycopene] and [leafy-greens]. Core component of [mediterranean-diet].
entries.caveats: Short trials use LDL oxidation markers rather than outcomes; PREDIMED was re-analysed after randomisation irregularities (results held). Phenolic content varies enormously between oils and labels rarely state it. In the 50-person OLIVAUS crossover, 60 mL/day of high- vs low-polyphenol oil for 3 weeks gave no significant between-treatment difference, with oxLDL falling only within the high-polyphenol arm (more in abdominal obesity), so effects in healthy people are modest. The throat sting of fresh oil comes from oleocanthal, a COX inhibitor with ibuprofen-like activity in vitro; its clinical relevance at culinary doses is unknown.

entries.title: Extra-virgin olive oil (high-phenolic)

entries.headline: In PCOS, intermittent fasting lowered weight (-4.25 kg) and free androgen index and raised SHBG, but no more than calorie restriction; in lean women a 72-h fast made 2 of 7 cycles anovulatory, and fasting beyond the overnight period in late pregnancy rapidly produces ketosis.

dose.effective: With PCOS and excess weight: an 8-10 h eating window or daily calorie restriction for 8+ weeks, whichever is easier to keep. Without excess weight: avoid deliberate energy deficit while trying to conceive.
dose.studied_range: 72-h follicular-phase fasts; 5-12 weeks of 6-10 h TRE in PCOS; Ramadan in pregnancy.
dose.too_much: Energy availability below ~30 kcal/kg lean mass/day disrupts LH pulses; multi-day fasts in lean women can block ovulation. In pregnancy avoid fasting beyond the overnight period (18-h fasts cause ketonaemia).
dose.timeframe: Androgen and menstrual changes in PCOS over 5-8 weeks; follicle effects within one cycle.
dose.notes: Normal-weight women tolerated a 3-day fast without cycle disruption; lean women (<=20% body fat) did not.

entries.mechanism: In insulin-resistant PCOS, lower insulin raises SHBG and lowers ovarian androgen output. In lean women, energy deficit slows GnRH/LH pulsatility (hypothalamic suppression). In pregnancy, 'accelerated starvation' raises maternal ketones that cross the placenta.
entries.interactions: Works through the same route as [weight-loss] in [pcos]. Stacking fasting with heavy training risks [vigorous-exercise-low-energy]. Prenatal nutrient needs (e.g., [folic-acid]) are harder to meet in short eating windows.
entries.caveats: PCOS evidence is five small studies; the only RCT comparing early TRE with calorie restriction (Talebi 2024) found no difference. Ramadan pregnancy meta-analyses show no birth-weight effect but are observational and lack mortality data; the IQ-ketone link (Rizzo 1991) is correlational.

key_numbers.label: Weight change with IF in PCOS (meta-analysis)
Energy availability threshold for LH disruption
PCOS women with improved menstrual regularity after 5 weeks of 8-h TRE

entries.title: Fasting, ovulation, PCOS and pregnancy

entries.headline: No trial shows fasting improves sperm; a 48-h fast cut LH by ~64% and lowered testosterone, 16:8 TRE lowered testosterone in trained men, and a retrospective IVF study found lower progressive motility (30% vs 38%) in samples produced during Ramadan.

dose.effective: None established. If overweight, the benefit comes from losing weight by any method; daily 12-14 h overnight fasts appear harmless.
dose.studied_range: 48-h fasts, 8 weeks of 16:8 TRE, Ramadan (dawn-to-sunset fasting for a month), three 5-day FMD cycles.
dose.too_much: Multi-day fasts suppress the reproductive axis within 48 h; avoid them during the ~74-day window before conception attempts or semen analysis.
dose.timeframe: Hormone changes within 48 h; semen effects would need one spermatogenic cycle (~74 days).
dose.notes: Ramadan meta-analysis found no average change in testosterone, LH or FSH, so daily dawn-to-dusk fasting is probably neutral for hormones.

entries.mechanism: Acute energy deficit slows hypothalamic GnRH/LH pulsatility and lowers testosterone and IGF-1; dehydration and circadian disruption during Ramadan may affect semen volume and motility.
entries.interactions: Weight loss in men with obesity improves semen quality; see [weight-loss] and [excess-adiposity]. Poor sleep during late-night eating periods overlaps with [short-sleep].
entries.caveats: Human sperm data are a 21-man 1986 study, a 97-man retrospective IVF cohort, and an 18-man FMD pilot. Rodent studies of fasting and sperm are not transferable.
entries.title: Fasting and sperm (Ramadan, TRE, multi-day fasts)

entries.headline: Three monthly 5-day cycles (~1,100 then ~700 kcal/day, low protein) lowered weight, trunk fat, blood pressure and IGF-1 vs usual diet in one 100-person trial; no direct oxidative stress endpoints, and the lead developer holds a commercial interest.

dose.effective: 5 consecutive days per month of a plant-based, low-protein, low-sugar, higher-unsaturated-fat diet (~1,100 kcal on day 1, ~700 kcal on days 2-5), for 3 cycles.
dose.studied_range: 3 monthly cycles in generally healthy adults; 3 cycles over 4 months in men with poor semen quality.
dose.too_much: Same exclusions as fasting: pregnancy, eating disorders, underweight, diabetes medication without supervision.
dose.timeframe: Changes measured after 3 cycles (3 months).
dose.notes: Benefits were concentrated in people with elevated baseline risk; low protein is probably what lowers IGF-1.

entries.mechanism: Mimics fasting signals (low insulin, IGF-1 and amino acids) while supplying some food; in mice, cycles triggered regeneration on refeeding and extended lifespan.
entries.interactions: Effects overlap with [weight-loss]; IGF-1 lowering is also achieved by moderate protein reduction under [calorie-restriction].
entries.caveats: Small number of trials, largely from one group with a commercial product; the 2.5-year 'biological age' reduction is an exploratory secondary analysis.
entries.title: Fasting-mimicking diet (5-day low-calorie, low-protein cycles)

entries.headline: Age is by far the dominant, non-modifiable driver of egg quality: fecundity falls from about 32 and faster after 37, and the share of women with no chromosomally normal embryo rises from 2-6% (age 26-37) to 33% at 42 and 53% at 44.

dose.effective: Not modifiable. The practical lever is time: ACOG/ASRM advise expedited evaluation after 6 months of trying from age 35, and immediate evaluation over 40.
dose.studied_range: Aneuploidy data from embryos of women aged ~22-47; egg chromosome-segregation data from ages 9-43.
dose.timeframe: Gradual decline from the early 30s, steep after ~37; no lifestyle change reverses it.
dose.notes: Lifestyle can avoid adding damage on top of age, but no diet or supplement has been shown to restore the chromosomal quality of older eggs in humans. Egg freezing at a younger age and IVF with PGT-A or donor eggs are the only interventions that address age directly.

entries.mechanism: Eggs are arrested in meiosis for decades. Cohesin that holds sister chromatids together is laid down before birth and is not renewed, so it erodes with age, causing chromosome mis-segregation (aneuploidy). In parallel, oocyte mitochondria become less efficient (less ATP, more mtDNA instability), CoQ10-synthesis enzymes and NAD+ levels decline (animal data), and spindle assembly becomes error-prone.
entries.interactions: Age magnifies almost every other harm: [tobacco-smoking] and [excess-adiposity] effects are layered on a declining baseline. Diet associations such as [mediterranean-diet] were seen only in women under 35 in one cohort. Supplements aimed at mitochondria ([coq10], [nmn-nad]) target the age mechanism but have no human live-birth proof.
entries.caveats: Aneuploidy also rises slightly in the very young (U-curve), but this is a minor effect compared with the rise after the mid-30s. Ovarian reserve tests (AMH, antral follicle count) predict egg number and response to stimulation, not egg quality; a woman with high AMH at 42 still has age-typical aneuploidy rates. Claims that any supplement 'reverses egg ageing' are not supported by human data.

entries.title: Female age (oocyte ageing)

factors.name: Fever and acute febrile illness (including flu, COVID-19)

entries.headline: A fever of 39-40 C for even 2 days can raise DNA fragmentation and cut sperm count for 2-3 months before recovering.

dose.effective: Body temperature around 38.5-40 C for 1 day or more.
dose.studied_range: Case report: 2 days at 39-40 C followed for 79 days.
dose.timeframe: DFI up 24-36% at days 15-37, back toward baseline by about day 79; plan semen tests or ART cycles at least ~3 months after a high fever if possible.
dose.notes: Fever control with paracetamol/acetaminophen is reasonable; there is no evidence that it prevents the sperm effect.

entries.mechanism: Whole-body hyperthermia warms the testes, impairing late spermatogenesis and chromatin protamination and increasing heat-shock and apoptotic signalling.
entries.interactions: Same mechanism as [sauna]. A semen test taken within 3 months of a fever may overstate long-term problems.
entries.caveats: Evidence is mostly case reports and small series; the effect is temporary.
entries.title: Fever and acute febrile illness (including flu, COVID-19)

factors.name: Fisetin (senolytic flavonol supplement; traces in strawberries)

entries.headline: Fisetin cleared senescent cells and extended lifespan in one mouse study, but the NIA Interventions Testing Program found no lifespan extension and no placebo-controlled senolytic trial in humans has reported results; food supplies milligrams, while trials test about 1.4 g doses.

dose.effective: None established.
dose.studied_range: Senolytic trials: 20 mg/kg/day for 2 consecutive days (about 1.4 g for a 70 kg adult), repeated intermittently; one small continuous trial used 200 mg/day for 12 weeks.
dose.too_much: High-dose human safety data are limited; flavonols alter the bioavailability of some drugs (see [quercetin]).
dose.notes: All flavonols and flavones together averaged about 17 mg/day in a Japanese diet, so eating strawberries cannot approach trial doses.

entries.mechanism: In cell and mouse models fisetin triggers apoptosis of senescent cells by disabling their anti-apoptotic defences, lowering the inflammatory SASP. Any antioxidant action in vivo is weak and short-lived.
entries.interactions: Same flavonol class as [quercetin]. The human senolytic data so far come from dasatinib plus quercetin, a drug combination, not from fisetin.
entries.caveats: The widely quoted mouse lifespan result was not reproduced by the multi-site ITP. The Mayo AFFIRM-LITE trial (started 2018) is still listed as enrolling in 2026. Senescent cells also help wound healing, so clearing them is not risk-free. The only completed RCTs are a small trial in obese men measuring adipokines and an unrelated stroke trial.

key_numbers.label: Total flavonol + flavone intake, Japanese women

entries.title: Fisetin (senolytic flavonol supplement; traces in strawberries)

entries.headline: The largest male supplement trial (FAZST, 2370 couples) found folic acid plus zinc did nothing for semen or live birth, and slightly raised DNA fragmentation.

dose.effective: Not recommended for male fertility.
dose.studied_range: 5 mg folic acid + 30 mg elemental zinc daily for 6 months.
dose.too_much: SDF 29.7% vs 27.2% with placebo (+2.4 points); more GI symptoms. Long-term zinc above ~40 mg/day can cause copper deficiency.
dose.timeframe: 6 months studied.
dose.notes: Correcting a genuine zinc or folate deficiency via diet is still sensible.

entries.mechanism: Folate supports one-carbon metabolism and DNA methylation; zinc stabilises sperm chromatin and is an antioxidant enzyme cofactor. High doses did not help replete men.
entries.interactions: High-dose folate overlaps with [high-dose-antioxidant-cocktail] concerns.
entries.caveats: Population was general infertility patients, not selected for deficiency.
entries.title: Folic acid + zinc

entries.headline: Folic acid is mandatory preconception care (400-800 ug/day prevents neural tube defects) and is also consistently associated with better fertility: 15% higher fecundability and 20 percentage points higher IVF live birth at > 800 ug/day supplemental folate.

dose.effective: 400-800 ug/day folic acid, started before conception (ideally 3 months ahead) and continued through early pregnancy.
dose.studied_range: Supplemental folate < 400 to > 800 ug/day (cohorts).
dose.too_much: Higher doses only on a clinician's advice for specific indications.
dose.timeframe: Before conception for neural tube protection; 3 months covers follicle development.
dose.notes: Usually taken as a prenatal multivitamin. Diet folate (leafy greens, legumes) is good but does not replace the supplement.

entries.mechanism: Folate supports one-carbon metabolism: DNA synthesis and repair, methylation and homocysteine clearance. Elevated homocysteine in follicular fluid is linked to poorer embryo quality.
entries.interactions: Core of [profertility-diet]; may buffer the [outdoor-air-pollution] association in one cohort.
entries.caveats: Fertility benefits are observational; the neural-tube benefit is RCT-proven and reason enough to take it.
entries.title: Folic acid / folate

entries.headline: Ejaculating every 1-2 days keeps sperm fresher: each extra day of abstinence adds about 0.65 points of SDF, and a second sample 3 hours after the first cut SDF from 35% to 24%.

dose.effective: Ejaculate (intercourse or otherwise) every 1-2 days through the fertile window and beyond. For ART with high SDF, ask about a sample after 1 day or a second sample 1-4 hours after a first ejaculation.
dose.studied_range: Abstinence from 1-4 hours to 7+ days; 2-day cut-off in RCT meta-analysis.
dose.too_much: Volume and total count fall with very frequent ejaculation, but for natural conception daily intercourse is not harmful.
dose.timeframe: Immediate: works on the next ejaculate.
dose.notes: Diagnostic labs usually specify 2-7 days of abstinence and SDF guidelines suggest 2-5 days before a test; follow the lab's instructions when testing, and use short abstinence for conception attempts and ART samples.

entries.mechanism: Shortens the time sperm sit in the epididymis, where defective sperm and leukocytes generate ROS and stored sperm accumulate oxidative DNA damage.
entries.interactions: Cheapest and fastest lever; a non-invasive alternative to [testicular-sperm-icsi]. Works alongside slower changes that act on sperm production.
entries.caveats: One large meta-analysis of risk factors found no significant abstinence effect, and absolute reductions in healthy men are small (about 2-3 points). The biggest drops are in men with high baseline SDF or abnormal semen.

key_numbers.label: SDF increase per extra day of abstinence
SDF in second sample 3 h later

entries.title: Frequent ejaculation (short abstinence, 1-2 days)

entries.headline: Doubling produce from 5.8 to 12 servings/day for 2 weeks reduced lymphocyte 8-OHdG and urinary isoprostanes, but another controlled trial found 600 g/day had no effect on oxidative DNA damage in healthy non-smokers; cohorts show lower mortality up to ~800 g/day.

dose.effective: At least 5 servings (400-500 g)/day, ideally up to ~800 g, from diverse botanical families.
dose.studied_range: 600 g/day for 24 days; 12 servings/day for 14 days.
dose.timeframe: Weeks.
dose.notes: Diversity across plant families mattered in the positive trial; benefit was larger in people with low baseline carotenoids.

entries.mechanism: Many compounds acting through different routes (Nrf2 electrophiles, gut metabolites, vitamin C/carotenoids, nitrate, fiber, potassium).
entries.interactions: The null Danish trial suggests healthy people with adequate defences may already be near a ceiling for oxidative DNA damage.
entries.caveats: Oxidative-marker trials conflict; cohort benefits may partly reflect healthier lifestyles.

key_numbers.label: All-cause mortality RR per 200 g/day fruit and vegetables

entries.title: High fruit and vegetable intake

entries.headline: Low-pesticide fruit and vegetables (2.8+ servings a day) are linked to much higher sperm counts; high-residue produce is not.

dose.effective: At least 3 servings/day; wash produce and favour lower-residue choices.
dose.studied_range: <1.1 to >=2.8 servings/day of low-to-moderate-residue produce.
dose.timeframe: ~3 months.
dose.notes: Benefit is likely part of the overall dietary pattern.

entries.mechanism: Food-level vitamin C, folate, carotenoids and polyphenols support seminal antioxidant defences without the megadoses that cause reductive stress.
entries.interactions: See [pesticides] and [mediterranean-diet].
entries.caveats: Total fruit and vegetable intake was unrelated to semen in the same study; the finding depended on pesticide residue classification.

key_numbers.label: Higher total count, >=2.8 servings/day low-residue produce

entries.title: Fruit and vegetables

entries.headline: Garlic supplements lower blood pressure in hypertensives (about -8.7/-6.1 mmHg) and a meta-analysis of 12 small RCTs reports lower MDA and higher antioxidant enzymes, but these markers are weak and the trials low quality.

dose.effective: Culinary: 1-2 cloves/day crushed and left 10 min before cooking; supplement trials used aged garlic extract or powder.
dose.studied_range: 80-4000 mg/day garlic preparations for 2-24 weeks.
dose.too_much: Supplements can increase bleeding risk with anticoagulants.
dose.timeframe: Weeks.
dose.notes: Red onions are a major dietary source of quercetin (onion chromatography total ~140 mg/100 g in Phenol-Explorer).

entries.mechanism: Organosulfur compounds (allicin breakdown products, S-allylcysteine) activate Nrf2 and raise hydrogen sulfide signalling; onion quercetin.
entries.interactions: Another mild Nrf2 inducer; much weaker than sulforaphane.
entries.caveats: TAC and TBARS-type MDA are non-specific oxidative markers; effect sizes in the meta-analysis (Hedges' g up to 13.8) are implausibly large, a sign of small heterogeneous studies.

key_numbers.label: Onion (red), total polyphenols, chromatography (sum of compounds)

entries.title: Garlic and onions

entries.headline: Active infection (e.g. Chlamydia, Mycoplasma) and white cells in semen raise ROS and SDF; treating a proven infection can lower SDF by about a third.

dose.effective: Leukocytospermia is defined as >=1 million white cells/mL; even 0.2-1 million/mL has been linked to higher ROS and SDF.
dose.studied_range: Antibiotic courses guided by culture/PCR; follow-up about 4 months.
dose.timeframe: In one study SDF fell from 37.7% to 24.2% after ~3.8 months of treatment; pregnancy rates were higher in couples who tried after rather than during treatment.
dose.notes: AUA/ASRM: if round cells exceed 1 million/mL, distinguish white cells from immature germ cells before treating. Treat confirmed infection; do not give empiric antibiotics for every abnormal semen test.

entries.mechanism: Activated neutrophils and macrophages produce superoxide via NADPH oxidase (NOX2) at rates far above sperm, overwhelming seminal antioxidants and attacking sperm membranes and DNA.
entries.interactions: [febrile-illness] from the same infection adds thermal damage. Antioxidants are not a substitute for treating infection.
entries.caveats: A large meta-analysis found overall effects of Chlamydia and HPV on SDF negligible, so the strongest data are from symptomatic or culture-positive cases. Evidence comes from small observational studies.
entries.title: Genital tract infection and leukocytospermia

entries.headline: In older adults with low glutathione, glycine plus NAC restored glutathione, lowered F2-isoprostanes and in a 24-person RCT improved mitochondrial, metabolic and physical-function measures. The trials are small and mostly from one group.

dose.effective: Glycine 1.33 mmol/kg/day + cysteine 0.81 mmol/kg/day as NAC (roughly 100 mg/kg glycine + 130 mg/kg NAC; ~7 g + ~9 g/day at 70 kg)
dose.studied_range: Same weight-based dose for 2 weeks to 24 weeks
dose.too_much: Long-term safety beyond 24 weeks not established; same cancer caveat as NAC.
dose.timeframe: Changes reported at 16-24 weeks; benefits declined within 12 weeks of stopping
dose.notes: Relevant mainly to older adults; young adults already have normal glutathione synthesis.

entries.mechanism: Supplies both limiting precursors (cysteine and glycine) for glutathione synthesis, which is reduced with aging. This restores GSH concentration and synthesis rate and lowers oxidative damage.
entries.interactions: Overlaps with [n-acetylcysteine]. Probably redundant in people with high protein intake and normal glutathione.
entries.caveats: Evidence comes from small open-label and placebo-controlled trials from a single research group, with no hard outcomes. The large doses are not those in typical over-the-counter products.
entries.title: Glycine + N-acetylcysteine (GlyNAC)

entries.headline: Four cups a day of decaffeinated green tea cut urinary 8-OHdG by 31% in heavy smokers over 4 months, and 4 cups/day lowered plasma MDA/HNE in metabolic syndrome; across 145 RCTs, flavan-3-ol foods including tea lower blood pressure by about 3/2 mmHg and improve FMD, while evidence on oxidative damage in healthy non-smokers stays weak.

dose.effective: About 4 cups (~1 L) per day of brewed green tea.
dose.studied_range: 4 cups/day for 8 weeks to 4 months.
dose.too_much: Brewed tea is considered safe at usual intakes (90-300 mg EGCG/day; heavy drinkers up to ~866 mg/day); rare idiosyncratic liver injury reported. See [green-tea-extract] for the supplement risk.
dose.timeframe: Weeks to months.
dose.notes: EGCG bioavailability is low and variable; plasma half-life ~3.4 h. Ring-fission valerolactone metabolites appear 3-15 h later.

entries.mechanism: Catechins (EGCG, EGC, EC) and their microbial valerolactone metabolites; at physiological doses mild Nrf2 signalling and effects on endothelium rather than plasma radical scavenging.
entries.interactions: Flavan-3-ols overlap with [cocoa-flavanols]. Tea with meals reduces non-heme iron absorption (relevant to [iron-excess] and to iron-deficient people). Unlike high-dose vitamins C and E, 980 mg/day of green-tea polyphenols did not appear to blunt antioxidant-enzyme adaptation in sprinters.
entries.caveats: The smoker trial used decaf tea and showed no benefit for black tea. Smokers have high baseline oxidative damage, so the effect may not generalise. Concentrated extracts are a different exposure: free EGCG exposure rose by more than 60% after 4 weeks of 800 mg once-daily dosing, and in a 12-month RCT in 1021 women, high-dose green tea extract caused moderate or worse liver-test abnormalities in 5.1% (see [green-tea-extract]).

key_numbers.label: Urinary 8-OHdG change in smokers (4 cups/day, 4 months)
Office systolic BP change, flavan-3-ol interventions (145 RCTs)

entries.title: Green tea (brewed)

entries.headline: 30 g/day of milled flaxseed for 6 months lowered systolic blood pressure by about 10 mmHg (15 mmHg in hypertensives) in a 110-patient RCT, one of the largest blood-pressure effects of any food; lignans and ALA both appear to contribute.

dose.effective: 30 g/day milled flaxseed (roughly 3-4 tablespoons).
dose.studied_range: 30 g/day in foods for 6 months.
dose.timeframe: Months.
dose.notes: Use milled seed; enterolignans rose 2-50-fold on the milled-flax diet.

entries.mechanism: Secoisolariciresinol diglucoside is converted by gut bacteria to enterodiol and enterolactone; ALA and its oxylipins also lower blood pressure. Plasma ALA tracked systolic and diastolic pressure, lignans tracked diastolic.
entries.interactions: ALA overlaps only partly with [omega3-fish]. Lignans also come from [whole-grains]. In PREDIMED, lignan intake was among the subclasses most strongly linked to lower mortality.
entries.caveats: One main RCT, in peripheral artery disease patients; replication in the general population is limited. Enterolactone production depends on the microbiome.
entries.title: Ground flaxseed (lignans plus alpha-linolenic acid)

entries.headline: Claims that touching the ground supplies 'antioxidant electrons' have no credible mechanism and rest on small, mostly unblinded studies by proponents.

dose.effective: Not recommended for oxidative stress. Walking barefoot outdoors is harmless and pleasant if you enjoy it.
dose.studied_range: Small studies of grounding mats/patches over nights to weeks.
dose.notes: No validated oxidative biomarker improvement in rigorous trials.

entries.mechanism: Proposed mechanism (free electrons neutralizing radicals) is not physiologically plausible: radical chemistry occurs inside cells and is buffered by enzymes and glutathione.
entries.interactions: None.
entries.caveats: The main review is by advocates; independent replication is lacking.
entries.title: Grounding / earthing

entries.headline: Chronic periodontitis is associated with lower systemic antioxidant capacity and higher malondialdehyde, and periodontal treatment lowers oxidative markers.

dose.effective: Brush twice daily, clean between teeth daily, and get professional cleaning and periodontal treatment if gums bleed or recede.
dose.studied_range: Non-surgical periodontal therapy studies with >=6 weeks follow-up.
dose.timeframe: Markers improved within 6 weeks to months after treatment.
dose.notes: Smoking and diabetes strongly worsen periodontitis.

entries.mechanism: Chronic bacterial infection recruits neutrophils that release superoxide, hypochlorous acid and other oxidants locally, with spill-over systemic inflammation.
entries.interactions: Worsened by [tobacco-smoking] and poor [glycemic-control].
entries.caveats: Most data are from saliva and gum fluid; systemic effects are less consistent and few trials are randomized.
entries.title: Gum disease (periodontitis)

entries.headline: Toxic metals deplete glutathione and drive oxidative damage; even at normal background levels, urinary cadmium tracked oxidative DNA damage in non-smokers.

dose.effective: Do not smoke (the main cadmium source); test well water for arsenic; check old homes for lead paint and pipes; choose low-mercury fish (salmon, sardines) over high-mercury species (swordfish, king mackerel, shark).
dose.studied_range: Observational studies at background and occupational exposure levels.
dose.too_much: Occupational exposures and contaminated water are the main high-dose risks.
dose.timeframe: Body burdens of cadmium and lead decline slowly (years).
dose.notes: Chelation 'detox' for people without documented poisoning is not supported.

entries.mechanism: Cadmium, lead and arsenic bind thiol groups, deplete glutathione and inhibit antioxidant enzymes; redox-active metals (iron, copper) generate hydroxyl radical via Fenton chemistry; arsenic can generate H2O2.
entries.interactions: Cadmium exposure is largely from [tobacco-smoking].
entries.caveats: Spot-urine biomarker studies are prone to confounding: in one study the strongest metal associations were for essential selenium and copper.
entries.title: Heavy metals: lead, cadmium, arsenic, mercury

entries.headline: Higher follicular-fluid mercury (above ~0.5 ug/L) and lead were associated with lower IVF live birth (lead RR 0.68) in a small study; cadmium exposure comes mainly from smoking.

dose.effective: Favour smaller, lower-mercury fish over large predatory fish (e.g. shark, swordfish); do not smoke (main cadmium source).
dose.studied_range: Follicular fluid Hg, Pb, Cd, As in 56 IVF patients.
dose.too_much: Follicular fluid Hg > ~0.51 ug/L associated with lower biochemical pregnancy and live birth.
dose.notes: Keep eating fish: the omega-3 benefit is real; choose low-mercury species.

entries.mechanism: Metals bind thiol groups, deplete glutathione and inactivate antioxidant enzymes; cadmium and lead can displace essential metals and promote Fenton-type ROS generation.
entries.interactions: Trades off against [omega3-fish] (fish is the main source of both); [tobacco-smoking] supplies cadmium.
entries.caveats: One small cohort; associations were non-linear and imprecise.

key_numbers.label: IVF live birth, higher follicular lead

entries.title: Heavy metals (mercury, lead, cadmium)

factors.name: Heavy vigorous exercise & low energy availability (women)

entries.headline: In lean women, 5 or more hours a week of vigorous exercise was associated with about 32% lower monthly chance of conception; exercising to exhaustion or on most days was linked to 2-3 times the odds of fertility problems.

dose.effective: If trying to conceive and lean, cap vigorous exercise below ~5 h/week and swap some for moderate activity; eat enough to keep regular cycles.
dose.studied_range: Vigorous activity 0 to >= 5 h/week (Danish cohort); frequency/intensity categories (Norwegian cohort).
dose.too_much: >= 5 h/week vigorous: FR 0.68 in lean women; exercising most days: 3.2-fold odds of fertility problems; exercising to exhaustion: 2.3-fold.
dose.timeframe: Cycle recovery after restoring energy balance can take months.
dose.notes: Missed or irregular periods in an active woman are a red flag for low energy availability (hypothalamic suppression).

entries.mechanism: Low energy availability suppresses GnRH pulsatility (functional hypothalamic amenorrhea), lowering estrogen and ovulation; this is an energy-signalling problem more than an oxidative one.
entries.interactions: No adverse association in women with BMI >= 25, for whom activity helps ([aerobic-exercise-moderate], [weight-loss]). Different from acute oxidative damage after ultra-endurance events ([overtraining-ultraendurance]); in general health, vigorous exercise in normal amounts is beneficial ([hiit-vigorous-exercise]).
entries.caveats: Observational and self-reported; vigorous exercise was not associated with worse IVF outcomes in the EARTH cohort.
entries.title: Very intense exercise and low energy availability (RED-S)

factors.name: Herbs and spices (oregano, rosemary, cloves, cinnamon, etc.)

entries.headline: Their biggest proven effect is in the pan: a polyphenol-rich spice mix cut malondialdehyde in cooked burgers by 71% and in the eaters' urine by 49%, and herb marinades cut heterocyclic amines in grilled steak by 57-88%.

dose.effective: Generous use in cooking, especially in meat dishes and marinades (about a tablespoon of dried herbs per meal); 14 g spice blend in a meal in one trial.
dose.studied_range: Single meals; marinating steaks 1 h before grilling at 204 °C.
dose.too_much: None established at culinary amounts.
dose.timeframe: Same meal.
dose.notes: Per gram, dried cloves, oregano and other herbs top every polyphenol table, but servings are small.

entries.mechanism: Rosmarinic acid, carnosic acid and carnosol inhibit lipid oxidation and Maillard/HCA chemistry in food and in the stomach, so fewer oxidized lipids are absorbed; a spice blend also lowered postprandial insulin and triglycerides.
entries.interactions: Counteracts [high-temperature-cooking] and [processed-red-meat] oxidation products. Here direct scavenging is plausible because the reaction happens in the food and gut, where concentrations are high.
entries.caveats: Meal studies are tiny (n=6-11) and short.

key_numbers.label: MDA reduction in spiced vs plain burger meat
Urinary MDA reduction after spiced burger
Total HCA reduction, Caribbean herb marinade

entries.title: Herbs and spices (oregano, rosemary, cloves, cinnamon, etc.)

entries.headline: In type 2 diabetes, urinary 8-iso-PGF2α tracked glucose variability (r = 0.86) and post-meal glucose, not HbA1c. Hyperglycaemia drives mitochondrial superoxide and AGE formation.

dose.effective: Limit post-meal glucose excursions and keep glucose in the normal range (see food and lifestyle areas).
dose.timeframe: Acute: postprandial window (hours); chronic: years
dose.notes: Dietary AGEs from dry-heat cooking add to the endogenous load (10- to 100-fold more than uncooked).

entries.mechanism: Excess glucose makes the mitochondrial ETC overproduce superoxide, which activates the polyol, AGE, PKC and hexosamine pathways. AGEs bind RAGE, activating NOX and NF-kB. Postprandial hyperglycaemia and hyperlipidaemia transiently raise oxidative stress and impair endothelial function.
entries.interactions: Compounds [excess-adiposity]. Antioxidants taken with a meal can attenuate postprandial oxidative stress, but this has not translated into supplement benefits.
entries.caveats: The Monnier study is small (21 patients). The extent to which glucose swings matter in non-diabetic people is less established.
entries.title: High blood glucose and post-meal glucose spikes

entries.headline: Type 2 diabetes was associated with ~75% higher urinary 8-iso-PGF2a, which tracked day-to-day glucose swings (r = 0.86) more than HbA1c; reducing glucose spikes is a meaningful lever.

dose.effective: Keep fasting glucose and HbA1c in the normal range (individualized targets with diabetes); limit post-meal spikes with fibre-rich whole foods, fewer refined carbohydrates, and a short walk after meals.
dose.studied_range: Case-control comparison using continuous glucose monitoring.
dose.too_much: Large post-meal excursions and sustained hyperglycemia.
dose.timeframe: Glucose swings respond within days; HbA1c over ~3 months.
dose.notes: Exercise and weight loss are the main non-drug tools.

entries.mechanism: High glucose overloads mitochondria, causing superoxide overproduction that activates the polyol, AGE, PKC and hexosamine pathways; AGE-RAGE binding further activates NADPH oxidase and NF-kB.
entries.interactions: Improved by [aerobic-exercise-moderate], [resistance-training], [weight-loss] and [short-sleep] correction.
entries.caveats: Monnier 2006 was small (21 patients); the 'swings matter more than average glucose' idea is supported mechanistically but outcome trials targeting variability are limited.
entries.title: Blood-sugar control and diabetes

entries.headline: Women with type 1 or type 2 diabetes have 24-36% lower fecundability; in mice, maternal diabetes damages oocyte mitochondria and raises egg aneuploidy.

dose.effective: Good glycaemic control before conception (managed with the diabetes team); weight loss and physical activity for insulin resistance.
dose.timeframe: Preconception optimisation over at least 3 months covers one full cycle of follicle growth.
dose.notes: Preconception glucose control is also critical for reducing birth-defect risk.

entries.mechanism: Hyperglycaemia increases mitochondrial superoxide and advanced glycation end-products; in diabetic mice oocytes show abnormal mitochondrial structure, lower ATP and TCA metabolites, spindle defects and aneuploidy, and the defective mitochondria are passed to the embryo.
entries.interactions: Overlaps with [excess-adiposity] and [pcos].
entries.caveats: Oocyte mechanism data are from animals; human data are fecundability associations.
entries.title: Diabetes and insulin resistance

entries.headline: Pooled over 78 RCTs, antioxidant supplements did not lower mortality and slightly raised it in low-bias trials (RR 1.04). A 20,536-person trial of vitamin E + C + beta-carotene found no effect at all. Around exercise they block training benefits.

dose.effective: None.
dose.studied_range: e.g. vitamin E 600 mg + C 250 mg + beta-carotene 20 mg/day (HPS); vitamin C 1,000 mg + E 400 IU/day (exercise studies)
dose.too_much: Any dose at these levels: no benefit; beta-carotene, vitamin A and vitamin E components carry the documented harms.
dose.timeframe: Exercise-blunting effect within 4 weeks; mortality signal over years
dose.notes: Raising blood vitamin levels does not mean oxidative damage was reduced; HPS raised levels 'substantially' with zero outcome change.

entries.mechanism: Suppresses ROS signals needed for adaptation (insulin sensitivity, mitochondrial biogenesis, endogenous antioxidant enzyme induction). In tumours, lowering ROS can release p53-dependent brakes and increase metastasis (mouse data). Endogenous enzymatic defences do not respond to extra dietary antioxidants once someone is replete.
entries.interactions: Antagonises the adaptive (hormetic) benefits of exercise. Contains [vitamin-e-supplement] and [beta-carotene-supplement] harms. Redundant with endogenous defences.
entries.caveats: Marketing often cites ORAC or 'total antioxidant capacity' values, which USDA abandoned in 2012 because they have no demonstrated in-vivo relevance.
entries.title: High-dose 'antioxidant formula' supplements (vitamin C + E + beta-carotene/A, etc.)

entries.headline: Too much antioxidant can loosen sperm chromatin: one study saw DFI fall 19% but decondensation rise 23%, and high doses damaged sperm DNA in mice.

dose.effective: Avoid taking several fertility products at once or doses well above the RDA (e.g. vitamin C >1 g, zinc >40 mg, folic acid >1 mg) without a specific indication.
dose.studied_range: Antioxidant vitamins with zinc and selenium for 90 days (human); dose-escalation of vitamin C, zinc, folate, carnitine (mice).
dose.too_much: This factor is the 'too much' end of [male-antioxidant-combination].
dose.timeframe: Over one spermatogenic cycle.
dose.notes: FAZST's small SDF increase with 5 mg folic acid + 30 mg zinc is consistent with this concern.

entries.mechanism: Sperm chromatin compaction depends on oxidative formation of protamine disulphide bridges in the epididymis, and capacitation needs a controlled ROS burst. Excess reductants (especially vitamin C) can reduce these disulphide bonds and blunt physiological ROS signalling.
entries.interactions: Opposes the benefits sought from [male-antioxidant-combination] and [vitamin-c-e-combined]; also relevant to [l-carnitine].
entries.caveats: Human evidence is one small uncontrolled study plus indirect trial data; the mouse data may not transfer. Plausible but unproven.
entries.title: Megadose or stacked antioxidants ('reductive stress')

factors.name: High-dose antioxidant supplements during training (vitamin C/E, resveratrol, NAC)

entries.headline: Gram-level vitamin C plus vitamin E, and 150-250 mg/day resveratrol, blunted molecular and some functional training adaptations in several RCTs (e.g. 45% smaller VO2max gain with resveratrol; lean-mass gain 1.4% vs 3.9% with C+E in older men), although meta-analyses find no significant loss of VO2max, endurance or strength overall.

dose.effective: Avoid routine supplementation at about 500-1000 mg/day vitamin C plus 235-400 IU vitamin E, or 150-250+ mg/day resveratrol, during training blocks. Get antioxidants from food. Correct true deficiencies (e.g. low vitamin C or low glutathione status) under guidance.
dose.studied_range: Vitamin C 500-1000 mg/day plus vitamin E 117.5-400 IU (4-12 weeks); resveratrol 150-250 mg/day (4-8 weeks); NAC 1200-2400 mg/day orally or IV infusion; quercetin ~1000 mg/day.
dose.too_much: 1000 mg vitamin C plus 400 IU vitamin E/day removed the insulin-sensitivity gain of 4 weeks' training in one trial; 1000 mg C plus 235 mg E blocked mitochondrial-protein gains and blunted bone-density gains in older men.
dose.timeframe: Effects appeared within 4-12 weeks of combined training and supplementation.
dose.notes: Timing has not been directly tested: blunting occurred both with daily dosing and when doses were taken just before and after sessions, so moving the pill a few hours away from workouts is not proven to help. Food-level intakes (fruit, vegetables, tea, cocoa) have not shown this effect. Acute NAC or other antioxidants before a single competition is a different question from chronic use during training.

entries.mechanism: Exercise ROS (largely NOX2-derived H2O2) act as second messengers that activate Nrf2, PGC-1alpha, MAPKs (p38, JNK, ERK) and insulin-signalling adaptations. Flooding cells with reducing agents can blunt this signal, reducing induction of SOD2, GPx, COX4 and mitochondrial biogenesis and hypertrophy signalling. Redundant pathways mean the blunting is partial and inconsistent.
entries.interactions: Directly undermines [aerobic-exercise-moderate], [hiit-vigorous-exercise] and [resistance-training]. See the general supplement entries [vitamin-c-supplement], [vitamin-e-supplement], [isolated-polyphenol-supplements], [n-acetylcysteine] and [high-dose-antioxidant-cocktail].
entries.caveats: Trials are small (11-54 people), use different doses and outcomes, and many find molecular blunting without performance loss. Isoflavones may even help lean-mass gains. NAC may help people with low glutathione.
entries.debate: Pro-blunting: vitamin C/E abolished insulin-sensitivity gains [exr-ristow2009], blocked mitochondrial-protein increases [exr-paulsen2014a, exr-gomezcabrera2008], blunted hypertrophy signalling [exr-paulsen2014b], lean-mass gains [exr-bjornsen2016] and bone gains in older men [exr-stunes2017]; resveratrol blunted VO2max, blood pressure and lipid improvements [exr-gliemann2013] and HIIT power gains [exr-scribbans2014], and impaired training effects on muscle oxidative and inflammatory markers [exr-olesen2014]; NAC infusion blunted adaptive signalling [exr-petersen2012]. Against: other RCTs found no effect on endurance adaptation or insulin sensitivity [exr-yfanti2010, exr-yfanti2011] or only partial cellular effects [exr-morrison2015]; a meta-analysis of 18 RCTs found no significant effect on VO2max (SMD -0.14), endurance, lean mass or strength [exr-clifford2020], and a strength-specific review found no effect on strength [exr-dutra2020]. Critics argued the resveratrol data do not show 'mainly negative' effects [exr-smoliga2013], and a polyphenol meta-analysis found resveratrol's harm non-significant (SMD -0.54) and isoflavones possibly helpful [exr-martineznegrin2022]. Underneath sits the question of whether exercise ROS are necessary at all: without any supplement, men with the smallest exercise-induced oxidative stress adapted least [exr-margaritelis2018], while reviews still weigh how essential the ROS signal is versus redundant pathways [exr-powers2024, exr-merry2016b]. A 'personalised' camp argues antioxidants help only deficient people: NAC improved performance only in men with low glutathione [exr-paschalis2018, exr-margaritelis2018b]. Narrative reviews converge on 'no benefit, possible harm' for chronic megadoses [exr-merry2016b, exr-mason2020, exr-higgins2020, exr-nikolaidis2012].

Smaller VO2max gain with 250 mg/day resveratrol

entries.title: High-dose antioxidant supplements during training (vitamin C/E, resveratrol, NAC)

entries.headline: EFSA (2018) concluded that 800 mg EGCG/day or more from supplements significantly raises liver transaminases in RCTs; extracts also cause rare severe liver injury, especially in multi-ingredient products.

dose.effective: No oxidative-stress benefit beyond brewed tea has been shown.
dose.studied_range: Supplements supply 5-1000 mg EGCG/day.
dose.too_much: >= 800 mg EGCG/day as a supplement (EFSA). Multi-ingredient products caused more severe injury.
dose.timeframe: Liver injury latency averaged ~6 months for green-tea-only products and ~6 weeks for multi-ingredient ones.
dose.notes: Brewed tea at traditional intakes is considered safe.

entries.mechanism: At high concentrations EGCG becomes pro-oxidant (generating H2O2) and hepatotoxic; patient susceptibility factors appear important.
entries.interactions: Do not combine with other hepatotoxic supplements.
entries.caveats: Absolute risk is low given wide use, but the dose threshold is clear from trials.

key_numbers.label: Typical EGCG from brewed green tea

entries.title: High-dose green tea extract (EGCG pills)

entries.headline: Dry heat (grilling, broiling, roasting, frying) raises food AGEs 10-100-fold; a high-AGE meal cut flow-mediated dilation by 36% vs 21% for the same meal cooked gently, and a year on a low-AGE diet improved insulin resistance and oxidative stress markers.

dose.effective: Favour moist heat (stewing, poaching, steaming), lower temperatures and shorter times; marinate meat in acidic, herb-rich mixtures.
dose.studied_range: Single meals (15,100 vs 2,750 kU AGE); 1-year low-AGE diet in 138 obese adults with metabolic syndrome; 12 dietary AGE RCTs (293 people).
dose.too_much: Charred, well-done meat is the main HCA/PAH source.
dose.timeframe: Vascular effects within 2 h of a meal; metabolic effects over months.
dose.notes: Acidic ingredients (lemon juice, vinegar) and moist heat significantly reduced new AGE formation. Animal foods high in fat and protein are most AGE-prone; vegetables, fruit and whole grains stay low even when cooked.

entries.mechanism: Maillard reactions form AGEs (e.g. CML) that engage RAGE and activate NADPH oxidase and NF-kB; meat creatine + sugars + amino acids form heterocyclic amines; fat dripping on flames forms PAHs.
entries.interactions: Pairs with [processed-red-meat]; reduced by [herbs-spices] marinades; compounded by [refined-sugar-high-glycemic] (endogenous AGE formation).
entries.caveats: Many dietary-AGE trials come from one research group; measurement of food AGEs by ELISA is debated. The systematic review rated evidence as limited by trial quality.

key_numbers.label: FMD fall after high-AGE meal (vs 20.9% low-AGE)

entries.title: High-temperature dry cooking (AGEs, HCAs, PAHs)

entries.headline: Cycling 5 or more hours a week is linked to lower sperm concentration; moderate cycling is not a concern.

dose.effective: Under about 5 hours/week is fine; above that, use a well-fitted saddle, padded shorts and rest days.
dose.studied_range: Cycling >=5 h/week vs no regular exercise (2261 men); 16 weeks of intensive road training (24 cyclists).
dose.too_much: Intensive training raised seminal inflammatory cytokines, with some semen changes persisting 30 days after stopping.
dose.timeframe: Recovery may need more than 30 days; plan ~3 months.
dose.notes: Combine with general exercise advice ([aerobic-exercise-moderate]).

entries.mechanism: Perineal pressure, scrotal heat and friction, plus inflammation and oxidative stress from very high training loads.
entries.interactions: Overlaps with [everyday-scrotal-heat].
entries.caveats: Observational; the training study comes from a group with several retracted papers.

key_numbers.label: Odds of low concentration, cycling >=5 h/week

entries.title: High-volume cycling

entries.headline: Being dehydrated increased muscle H2O2 after resistance exercise in one small study; there is no evidence that drinking extra water beyond thirst lowers oxidative stress.

dose.effective: Drink to thirst; aim for pale-yellow urine; replace fluids lost in heavy sweating.
dose.studied_range: One crossover study with 24 h fluid restriction.
dose.too_much: Overdrinking (hyponatremia) is a risk in endurance events.
dose.notes: 'Alkaline' or 'structured' water claims have no support.

entries.mechanism: Dehydration raises cell stress and may increase ROS production in exercising muscle.
entries.interactions: Relevant to [overtraining-ultraendurance] and [sauna].
entries.caveats: Evidence is a single small study; 'flushing out toxins' with water is not a real antioxidant mechanism.
entries.title: Hydration

entries.headline: Molecular hydrogen scavenges hydroxyl radicals in lab and animal studies, but human trials are small and show at most modest effects on lipids, not established oxidative-stress benefits.

dose.effective: Not recommended for oxidative stress. Trials used ~0.5-1.5 L/day of hydrogen-rich water.
dose.studied_range: Pilot RCTs of weeks to 6 months.
dose.too_much: Appears safe.
dose.notes: Hydrogen escapes quickly from water once opened.

entries.mechanism: H2 reacts selectively with hydroxyl radical and peroxynitrite; may also signal via Nrf2. Doses from drinking water are tiny and transient.
entries.interactions: No known interactions.
entries.caveats: Most trials are small and come from a few research groups; the telomere result came from a 40-person pilot with many outcomes, and the lipid meta-analysis pooled only 7 small studies.
entries.title: Hydrogen-rich water / molecular hydrogen

entries.headline: Fitness is one of the strongest predictors of survival: each 1-MET higher VO2max (about 3.5 mL/kg/min) is associated with 11-17% lower mortality, and the least fit have about 4x the risk of the most fit, with no upper limit; but genetic analyses question how much of this is caused by fitness itself.

dose.effective: Aim to move out of the bottom fifth for your age and sex, then keep improving: each +1 MET counts. Combine 150+ min/week of aerobic activity with 1-2 weekly interval sessions (e.g. 4 x 4 min at 85-95% HRmax); add sessions or intensity if fitness does not budge.
dose.studied_range: Cohorts: fitness from under 5 to over 14 METs on treadmill tests; training studies: 60-300 min/week for 6-24 weeks.
dose.too_much: No upper limit of benefit was seen for measured fitness, even at the 98th percentile (elite).
dose.timeframe: VO2max rises measurably within 4-8 weeks of training; fitness change over years tracks mortality.
dose.notes: The lowest mortality in 750,302 veterans was at about 14 METs (roughly 49 mL/kg/min). In older adults (70-77 years), being moderately fit gave most of the benefit. 'Non-responders' to standard programs responded when weekly time or intensity was raised.

entries.mechanism: Training raises stroke volume, blood and haemoglobin volume, capillary density and muscle mitochondrial content (PGC-1alpha), via the same redox-signalling and hormesis pathways as [aerobic-exercise-moderate]. High fitness travels with lower blood pressure, visceral fat, insulin resistance and inflammation, all chronic ROS sources.
entries.interactions: Built by [aerobic-exercise-moderate], [hiit-vigorous-exercise] and even [exercise-snacks]; strength gains appear to feed fitness ([resistance-training]). Lower body fat raises VO2max per kg ([weight-loss]).
entries.caveats: Baseline fitness and trainability partly reflect genes, body composition and health status, so people with undiagnosed disease test as 'unfit'. Most data come from people referred for treadmill tests. VO2max in mL/kg/min also falls with fat mass, so part of the signal is adiposity.
entries.debate: Proponents point to large, consistent cohorts with graded associations and no upper limit [exr-mandsager2018, exr-kokkinos2022, exr-kodama2009, exr-han2022, exr-lang2024], an AHA call to treat fitness as a vital sign [exr-ross2016], and evidence that improving fitness over time tracks lower mortality [exr-imboden2019]. Skeptics note that a two-sample Mendelian randomization found genetically predicted VO2max was not causally associated with longevity, while activity, lean mass and lower fat did raise VO2max [exr-kjaergaard2025], that genetic analyses point from strength to fitness rather than the reverse [exr-norris2024], that the certainty of the meta-analytic evidence is very low to moderate [exr-lang2024], and that the only long-term exercise RCT in older adults did not reduce mortality significantly [exr-stensvold2020]. In older adults, benefit may plateau above moderate fitness [exr-tari2025]. Trainability is also debated: non-response to standard doses disappears at higher doses [exr-montero2017] or intensities [exr-ross2015].

Mortality HR, elite vs low performers

entries.headline: I3C (200-400 mg/day) and DIM reliably shift estrogen metabolism toward 2-hydroxylation, and I3C regressed cervical precancer in one 30-woman trial, but no trial shows fewer cancers, DIM lowered active tamoxifen metabolites, and high-dose I3C caused liver tumours in male mice and uterine cancer in female rats.

dose.effective: No outcome-based dose; 200-400 mg/day I3C or 300 mg/day DIM shifted estrogen metabolites.
dose.studied_range: I3C 200-1200 mg/day; DIM 150 mg twice daily for up to 12 months.
dose.too_much: Do not combine with tamoxifen (endoxifen fell). NTP found carcinogenicity at high gavage doses. DIM plasma levels plateau above about 1000 mg I3C.
dose.timeframe: Estrogen metabolite shift within 1 month.
dose.notes: I3C itself never reaches the blood; it condenses in stomach acid, and DIM is the only product detected in plasma. Eating crucifers gives a much smaller version of the same shift.

entries.mechanism: Acid-condensation products of I3C (chiefly DIM) activate the aryl hydrocarbon receptor and induce CYP1A enzymes that hydroxylate estradiol at C-2 rather than C-16; they are also weak Nrf2 inducers.
entries.interactions: Synergistic or additive with isothiocyanates (sulforaphane, PEITC) in cell Nrf2 assays. Food sources overlap [cruciferous-other] and [broccoli-mature]. Drug interaction with tamoxifen.
entries.caveats: The urinary 2:16-hydroxyestrone ratio is a surrogate with an uncertain link to cancer risk. The cervical trial is small and unreplicated. Higher catechol-estrogen levels could have long-term downsides. Marketing for 'estrogen detox' outruns the data.

key_numbers.label: Complete CIN regression on I3C (8 of 17) vs placebo (0 of 10)
Plasma DIM Cmax plateau (1000 mg I3C)

entries.title: Indole-3-carbinol (I3C) and DIM supplements

factors.name: Indoor combustion: wood stoves, fireplaces, gas cooking

entries.headline: Wood smoke at smoky-home levels raised airway oxidative stress in one chamber study but had no systemic effect in another; gas cooking is linked to childhood asthma, though the quality of that evidence is debated.

dose.effective: Use range hoods vented outdoors when cooking (especially on gas), keep wood stoves well-sealed and burning cleanly, avoid open fireplaces as daily heat, and ventilate.
dose.studied_range: Chamber studies: 3-4 h at 220-354 µg/m³ wood-smoke particles.
dose.too_much: Exposure in poorly vented homes with daily solid-fuel burning (much higher in low-income countries using biomass).
dose.timeframe: Airway markers changed within hours.
dose.notes: Electric or induction cooking removes the NO2 source.

entries.mechanism: Combustion particles and gases (NO2, aldehydes, PAHs) generate airway ROS and inflammation; NO2 is itself an oxidant.
entries.interactions: Similar pathways to [outdoor-air-pollution]; mitigated by [hepa-air-purifier] for particles.
entries.caveats: Controlled wood-smoke studies are small and inconsistent. The gas-stove literature is mostly cross-sectional; a 2013 meta-analysis found OR 1.32 for asthma while a 2023 review judged the evidence too low-quality for causal conclusions.
entries.title: Indoor combustion: wood stoves, fireplaces, gas cooking

entries.headline: In randomized sham-controlled crossover trials, running HEPA purifiers cut indoor PM2.5 by about half and lowered oxidative and inflammatory markers (8-isoprostane, myeloperoxidase) and blood pressure within days.

dose.effective: Run a HEPA purifier sized for the room (check its clean-air delivery rate) continuously in the bedroom and main living space when outdoor or indoor PM2.5 is elevated, with windows closed.
dose.studied_range: Trials: 48 h to 1 week of real vs sham purification in dormitories with outdoor PM2.5 roughly 40-100 µg/m³.
dose.timeframe: Effects within 48 h to 1 week; they disappear when purification stops.
dose.notes: Benefits are largest where indoor air is polluted; in clean-air regions the gain is small.

entries.mechanism: Removes redox-active particles before they reach the lungs, reducing airway NADPH-oxidase activation, inflammatory cell activation and systemic lipid peroxidation.
entries.interactions: Counters [outdoor-air-pollution] and [indoor-combustion-smoke]; does not remove gases like NO2 unless the unit has activated carbon.
entries.caveats: Trials were short, in young healthy Chinese students exposed to high pollution; long-term clinical outcomes are not yet shown.
entries.title: Indoor HEPA air purification

entries.headline: Industrial trans fats raise LDL, lower HDL, promote systemic inflammation and endothelial dysfunction, and carry a higher coronary risk per gram than any other fat.

dose.effective: As close to zero as possible from partially hydrogenated oils.
dose.studied_range: Cohorts and controlled feeding studies.
dose.too_much: Any regular intake from partially hydrogenated oils.
dose.timeframe: Years.
dose.notes: Now banned or restricted in many countries; still present in some imported or older products.

entries.mechanism: Altered lipoprotein metabolism and inflammatory signalling (NF-kB), endothelial dysfunction.
entries.interactions: Often co-occurs with [oxidized-frying-oils] in fried fast food.
entries.caveats: The oxidative-stress component is one part of a broader cardiometabolic harm.
entries.title: Industrial trans fats

entries.headline: Intermittent fasting helps mainly by making people eat less: across 99 RCTs it beat ad libitum eating, but matched calorie restriction about equally (Cochrane: -0.56 kg difference over 3-12 months), and calorie-matched trials show no fasting-specific drop in oxidative stress markers.

dose.effective: Any form you can sustain that produces a modest energy deficit: an 8-10 h daily eating window, alternate-day fasting (~500 kcal or zero on fast days), or 2 days/week of 500-600 kcal (5:2). See [time-restricted-eating], [alternate-day-fasting], [five-two-diet].
dose.studied_range: Daily fasts of 12-20 h, 24-36 h alternate-day fasts, 2 days/week at ~25% of needs, for 3 weeks to 12 months.
dose.too_much: Daily eating windows under ~6 h and multi-day fasts increase lean-mass loss; not for pregnancy, eating disorders, underweight, type 1 diabetes, or insulin/sulfonylurea users without medical adjustment.
dose.timeframe: Weight and insulin changes within 4-12 weeks; oxidative stress markers follow weight loss.
dose.notes: Fasting length matters physiologically (ketones barely rise before ~20 h), but for health outcomes the total energy deficit matters far more than the pattern.

entries.mechanism: Energy deficit and weight loss lower insulin, adipose inflammation and mitochondrial ROS production. Longer fasts add a metabolic switch to fatty acids and ketones; beta-hydroxybutyrate can inhibit class I HDACs and induce FOXO3A and metallothionein (mouse data). Early eating windows align intake with circadian insulin sensitivity.
entries.interactions: Effects largely overlap with [calorie-restriction] and [weight-loss]; benefits are biggest with [excess-adiposity] and [glycemic-control] problems. Pair with [resistance-training] and adequate protein to limit lean loss. Diet quality still matters: fasting does not offset [overfeeding] on eating days. Late, short windows can shorten sleep; see [short-sleep].
entries.caveats: Most claims about autophagy, 'cellular cleanup' and longevity come from rodents. Calorie-matched trials (Templeman 2021, Liu 2022, Peters 2025) found no fasting-specific benefit. Only modified alternate-day fasting for BMI reached high-quality evidence in an umbrella review, and IF is associated with fat-free mass loss. The early eTRF oxidative stress result (n = 8) was driven partly by worsening on the control schedule.

key_numbers.label: IF vs continuous restriction, weight at 3-12 months (Cochrane)
ADF vs continuous restriction, weight (network meta-analysis)

entries.title: Intermittent fasting (umbrella: TRE, alternate-day, 5:2, periodic)

entries.headline: IV glutathione is cleared from blood with a half-life of ~14 minutes; oral glutathione raised blood stores 17-35% in one 6-month RCT, but no trial shows clinical benefit for oxidative stress.

dose.effective: Not recommended. Oral trial used 250-1000 mg/day for 6 months; levels returned to baseline within a month of stopping.
dose.studied_range: IV: single 2 g/m² infusion pharmacokinetics; oral: 6-month RCT.
dose.too_much: No benefit shown; usual infusion risks apply to IV use.
dose.timeframe: IV effect gone within about an hour; oral effect builds over months and reverses within a month.
dose.notes: Cells make their own glutathione from cysteine, glycine and glutamate; exercise, sleep and not smoking support it.

entries.mechanism: Exogenous glutathione is broken down in plasma and by gamma-glutamyl transferase into amino acids; cells resynthesize glutathione internally.
entries.interactions: Lifestyle factors that preserve glutathione: avoiding [tobacco-smoking] and [alcohol], [short-sleep] correction.
entries.caveats: Biomarker increases do not equal health benefit; no outcome trials.
entries.title: Intravenous (IV) or oral glutathione

entries.headline: Polyphenols reach only about 0-4 µmol/L in plasma, mostly as metabolites. Effects in human trials are small and mostly on biomarkers, and no outcome benefit is established for capsules.

dose.effective: Not established for outcomes.
dose.studied_range: Tens to hundreds of mg/day in short biomarker studies
dose.timeframe: Transient plasma exposure after each dose
dose.notes: Bioavailability varies over 100-fold by compound (urinary recovery 0.3-43%); isoflavones and gallic acid are best absorbed, proanthocyanidins and anthocyanins worst.

entries.mechanism: Direct scavenging in plasma is implausible at these concentrations. Likely actions are mild electrophilic Nrf2 activation, modulation of NF-kB and endothelial signalling, and local effects in the gut, where much of the dose and its microbial metabolites act.
entries.interactions: May act additively with other Nrf2 activators in vitro; human interaction data are lacking. The rise in plasma antioxidant capacity after polyphenol foods is mostly uric acid.
entries.caveats: Cell-culture 'antioxidant' effects are often artefacts of polyphenols oxidising in culture media. Whole foods with the same polyphenols carry fibre and other components.

key_numbers.label: Peak plasma metabolites per 50 mg dose

entries.title: Isolated polyphenol capsules (quercetin, resveratrol, grape-seed, etc.)

entries.headline: Cutting carbohydrate to roughly 20-50 g/day raises blood beta-hydroxybutyrate to about 0.5-3 mmol/L; it is a proven epilepsy therapy and lowers HbA1c, triglycerides and CRP in the short term, but direct evidence that it lowers oxidative damage in humans is thin, and LDL/apoB can rise sharply in lean people.

dose.effective: Under ~20-50 g/day total carbohydrate (about 5-10% of energy), protein around 1.2-2 g/kg, fat to appetite; aim for blood BHB 0.5-3 mmol/L. Build it around non-starchy vegetables, olive oil, nuts, seeds, fish, eggs and avocado rather than processed meat and butter.
dose.studied_range: Epilepsy: classic 4:1 diet or modified Atkins 10-20 g/day carbohydrate for >= 3 months. Type 2 diabetes: < 20-50 g/day for 6 months to 5 years. Weight/metabolic trials: 2 weeks to 2 years.
dose.too_much: Ketoacidosis needs BHB >= 3 mmol/L plus acidosis; healthy people on diet alone rarely exceed ~3 mmol/L, but SGLT2-inhibitor users, people with type 1 diabetes, and breastfeeding women can tip into ketoacidosis. Not for pregnancy or trying to conceive without specialist care, fatty-acid oxidation disorders, pyruvate carboxylase deficiency, porphyria, eating disorders, or people on insulin or sulfonylureas without medication adjustment.
dose.timeframe: Ketones rise within days (a fast alone gives ~1 mmol/L by 24-48 h), and stable ketosis was confirmed at ~4 weeks in one RCT. Muscle fat-oxidation adaptation takes 5-6 days to a few weeks, glycaemic effects take weeks, and seizure benefit is judged at ~3 months.
dose.notes: Fingerstick blood BHB is the reference measurement. Breath acetone is a reasonable non-invasive proxy. Urine strips read only acetoacetate, fade as the kidney adapts, and are best in early-morning or post-dinner urine. Check lipids including apoB at baseline and 6-12 weeks.

entries.mechanism: Low insulin releases fatty acids that the liver converts to acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate (BHB). In cells and mice, BHB inhibits class I HDACs, which up-regulates FOXO3a, MT2, catalase and MnSOD. This result failed to replicate in one cell study. BHB also blocks NLRP3 inflammasome assembly and activates HCAR2 (GPR109A). Ketone oxidation shifts the mitochondrial NAD and coenzyme Q redox couples. In rats, ketogenic feeding causes a brief burst of mitochondrial H2O2 and 4-HNE that activates Nrf2 and raises glutathione, which looks like hormesis. In humans the clearer routes are lower glucose and insulin, fewer glycaemic excursions, weight loss and lower triglycerides. High fatty-acid supply can raise mitochondrial H2O2 emission, and acetoacetate can generate superoxide in vitro.
entries.interactions: Overlaps heavily with [calorie-restriction] and [intermittent-fasting] because all three raise ketones and cause weight loss. Most metabolic benefit runs through [weight-loss] and better [glycemic-control], and through removing [refined-sugar-high-glycemic] foods. Against [mediterranean-diet], the crossover trial found equal HbA1c, but keto raised LDL and cut fibre. A Mediterranean-style keto (olive oil, fish, vegetables) is the reasonable middle ground. Usually lowers fibre and bifidobacteria, working against [dietary-fiber-microbiome]. Impairs high-intensity endurance economy, so it is a poor fit for competitive [hiit-vigorous-exercise] or racing; [aerobic-exercise-moderate] and [resistance-training] are maintained. BHB and sulforaphane ([broccoli-sprouts]) both act on HDACs and Nrf2 in lab models. That overlap is an inference: no human data show synergy or redundancy. In PCOS see [ketogenic-diet]. For a less restrictive option see [low-carb-diet].
entries.caveats: Human oxidative-stress data are small and short. In 20 women, 2 weeks raised total antioxidant status but did not change MDA, SOD or catalase. Children on the diet had higher brain glutathione, but that study was cross-sectional. In an isocaloric metabolic-ward study keto did not speed fat loss, and in an inpatient crossover people ate ~690 kcal/day more on animal-based keto than on a plant-based low-fat diet. Weight-loss advantage over low-fat diets is about 1 kg at a year. Diabetes benefits are largest at 3-6 months and fade by 12 months in RCT pooling. The Virta data are non-randomised. LDL rose about 41 mg/dL in lean people and fell in people with BMI >= 35. The 'lean mass hyper-responder' coronary-plaque data are cross-sectional, and the follow-up paper that claimed apoB did not predict plaque progression was retracted in 2026. Animal-based low-carb patterns are associated with higher mortality and plant-based ones with lower. Other risks: kidney stones (~6%), thiamine, folate, magnesium and iodine gaps, constipation, and poorer bone-turnover markers in athletes. Unhealthy versions (processed meat, little fibre) undo much of the case.

Extra ad libitum intake vs plant-based low-fat
Children with >50% seizure reduction (keto vs control)

entries.title: Ketogenic diet (nutritional ketosis)

entries.headline: In men with obesity, very-low-calorie ketogenic diets raised total testosterone by ~6.75 nmol/L (normocaloric keto by ~1 nmol/L), in proportion to weight lost. No human trial has measured semen quality on keto; the only semen data are from obese mice.

dose.effective: Weight loss via a supervised very-low-calorie ketogenic diet (8-14 weeks) in men with obesity-related low testosterone, then a sustainable diet.
dose.studied_range: 7 studies, 230 participants; mostly uncontrolled before-after designs of 8-14 weeks.
dose.too_much: Rapid weight loss and very-low-calorie protocols need medical supervision. LDL may rise in lean men.
dose.timeframe: Testosterone changes within 8-12 weeks; any semen effect would need at least one ~74-day spermatogenic cycle.
dose.notes: Probably a weight-loss effect rather than a ketone effect. Higher-fat diets keep testosterone a little higher than low-fat diets (SMD ~0.38), independent of keto.

entries.mechanism: Weight loss lowers aromatase activity and insulin resistance, which releases hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal suppression. In obese mice an MCT-based ketogenic diet lowered testicular lipid peroxidation and raised glutathione peroxidase.
entries.interactions: Essentially a subset of [weight-loss] / [excess-adiposity]. General effects are under [ketogenic-diet].
entries.caveats: No controlled human semen data. The testosterone meta-analysis pools mostly uncontrolled studies, and the gains track weight loss and age. The animal data compare keto with a high-fat high-cholesterol obesogenic diet, not with a healthy diet.
entries.title: Ketogenic diet (male fertility)

entries.headline: In overweight women with PCOS, ketogenic and low-carb diets cut weight (~5 kg more than other diets), LH and insulin resistance and appear to improve cycles and ovulation. In mice, though, ketone levels typical of keto slow embryo development and a gestational keto diet harms offspring, so the case for staying ketotic while trying to conceive is weak.

dose.effective: For overweight PCOS: 8-12 weeks of a ketogenic diet (< 20-50 g/day carbohydrate, often Mediterranean-style) or a moderate low-carbohydrate diet (< 45% of energy) aimed at weight loss. Then move to a sustainable lower-glycaemic diet with folate-rich foods plus a folic-acid supplement before trying to conceive.
dose.studied_range: PCOS trials: 45 days to 24 weeks, ketogenic (< 20-50 g/day) and very-low-energy ketogenic protocols; low-carb RCTs < 45% energy for > 4 weeks.
dose.too_much: Not recommended once trying to conceive or in pregnancy outside specialist care (epilepsy). Avoid in lean PCOS without weight to lose. Restricted carbohydrate intake was linked to half the dietary folic acid and 30% higher odds of neural tube defects.
dose.timeframe: Hormonal and menstrual changes over 8-24 weeks, alongside weight loss.
dose.notes: Grade honestly: most PCOS data are uncontrolled before-after studies or small RCTs. Pregnancy and live-birth data are anecdotal (2 conceptions in an 11-woman pilot). Benefits are hard to separate from weight loss.

entries.mechanism: Lower insulin reduces ovarian theca androgen production and raises SHBG. Weight loss lowers adipose inflammation and lipotoxicity. In PCOS mice, BHB reduced granulosa-cell inflammation and apoptosis. Against that, BHB at ~2 mmol/L (keto-diet levels) disturbed embryo glycolysis and histone acetylation and reduced viability in mouse embryo culture. A maternal keto diet raised BHB in oviduct fluid and delayed blastocyst development.
entries.interactions: Works through [weight-loss] and [glycemic-control]; see [pcos] / [pcos]. Can be combined with [myo-inositol]. Folate intake drops when grains are cut, so pair with [folic-acid]. General-health effects are under [ketogenic-diet] and [low-carb-diet].
entries.caveats: Meta-analyses (2019-2026) agree on weight, insulin and LH but are inconsistent on androgens and lipids, with high heterogeneity. Two RCTs found no weight advantage over a matched low-calorie diet. Low-carb diets help reproductive outcomes in pooled PCOS RCTs, but the evidence is mostly not specific to ketosis. There are no human oocyte-quality data. The cautionary data (embryo, gestation, offspring lifespan) are mouse studies at diets more extreme than human keto, and the neural-tube association is observational.

key_numbers.label: Weight change vs other diets in PCOS
Ovulatory infertility RR, highest vs lowest carb intake

entries.title: Ketogenic / low-carbohydrate diet (PCOS and conception)

entries.headline: Carnitines improve sperm motility and morphology in small trials, with no demonstrable effect on pregnancy; very high doses damaged sperm DNA in mice.

dose.effective: 1-2 g/day L-carnitine (often with 0.5-1 g acetyl-L-carnitine) for 3-6 months.
dose.studied_range: 8 RCTs, mostly 2 g/day L-carnitine + 1 g acetyl-L-carnitine.
dose.too_much: In healthy mice, moderate-to-high carnitine doses caused severe sperm DNA fragmentation and lower pregnancy rates (reductive stress).
dose.timeframe: 3-6 months.
dose.notes: Can cause fishy body odour and GI upset; raises TMAO.

entries.mechanism: Transports fatty acids into mitochondria for sperm energy; antioxidant properties in the epididymis.
entries.interactions: Included in MOXI (1 g), which was null. See [high-dose-antioxidant-cocktail].
entries.caveats: Small, heterogeneous trials; pregnancy not improved.
entries.title: L-carnitine / acetyl-L-carnitine

entries.headline: Evidence for women is weak; the most-cited positive RCT (L-carnitine 3 g/day in clomiphene-resistant PCOS) has been retracted.

dose.effective: No proven dose for female fertility.
dose.studied_range: 3 g/day in the retracted PCOS trial.
dose.notes: Male-factor evidence is separate and somewhat better.

entries.mechanism: Shuttles long-chain fatty acids into mitochondria for beta-oxidation, which oocytes use for energy.
entries.interactions: Included in [female-antioxidant-supplements] analyses.
entries.caveats: Retraction of the main trial removes the main human evidence.
entries.title: L-carnitine / acetyl-L-carnitine

factors.name: Laptops on the lap, tight underwear, long sitting, occupational heat

entries.headline: Everyday heat sources raise scrotal temperature 1-3 C; boxer wearers have about 25% higher sperm concentration, but direct SDF data are thin.

dose.effective: Laptop on a desk, not the lap; looser underwear (boxers); stand or walk for a few minutes every 30-60 min; heat protection or breaks for hot jobs (bakers, welders, drivers).
dose.studied_range: Laptop sessions of 60 min; scrotal temperature +1 C within 11-28 min.
dose.too_much: A laptop on closed thighs raised scrotal temperature 2.6-2.8 C in 60 min; lap pads did not prevent it.
dose.timeframe: Benefits, if any, would appear after one spermatogenic cycle (~3 months).
dose.notes: Sitting with legs apart reduces the rise. Heated car seats are plausible but unstudied for sperm.

entries.mechanism: Mild, repeated scrotal hyperthermia: same thermal pathway as saunas but smaller in size.
entries.interactions: Additive with [sauna] and [varicocele].
entries.caveats: Underwear and laptop data are cross-sectional or physiological (temperature) studies; the underwear association was partly explained by FSH. Occupational heat is a recognised risk but studies are older and confounded.
