pmid:32517172.finding: A 10-day Buchinger fast lowered plasma TBARS and raised total antioxidant capacity alongside rising uric acid; erythrocyte GSH, GR, GPx and catalase were unchanged.

pmid:35194047.authors: Xie Z, Sun Y, Ye Y, et al.
pmid:35194047.title: Randomized controlled trial for time-restricted eating in healthy volunteers without obesity.
pmid:35194047.finding: 5 weeks of early TRE improved insulin sensitivity, fasting glucose, adiposity and inflammation more than mid-day TRE.

pmid:24492839.authors: Paulsen G, Cumming KT, Holden G, et al.
pmid:24492839.title: Vitamin C and E supplementation hampers cellular adaptation to endurance training in humans: a double-blind, randomised, controlled trial.
pmid:24492839.finding: 1000 mg vitamin C plus 235 mg vitamin E daily for 11 weeks of endurance training did not change VO2max gains (8% in both groups) but blunted training-induced increases in muscle mitochondrial markers.

pmid:21325105.authors: Yfanti C, Nielsen AR, Akerström T, et al.
pmid:21325105.title: Effect of antioxidant supplementation on insulin sensitivity in response to endurance exercise training.
pmid:21325105.finding: 500 mg vitamin C plus 400 IU vitamin E during 12 weeks of intense endurance training (5x/week) did not change the ~17-19% training-induced gain in insulin-stimulated glucose uptake or VO2max.

pmid:26129928.authors: Bjørnsen T, Salvesen S, Berntsen S, et al.
pmid:26129928.title: Vitamin C and E supplementation blunts increases in total lean body mass in elderly men after strength training.
pmid:26129928.finding: 500 mg vitamin C plus 117.5 mg vitamin E around each of three weekly strength sessions for 12 weeks blunted lean-mass gain (1.4% vs 3.9% on placebo) but not strength gains.

pmid:31851538.authors: Clifford T, Jeffries O, Stevenson EJ, et al.
pmid:31851538.title: The effects of vitamin C and E on exercise-induced physiological adaptations: a systematic review and Meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
pmid:31851538.finding: Across 9 aerobic and 9 resistance-training RCTs, vitamin C and/or E did not significantly attenuate gains in VO2max, endurance performance, lean mass or strength; trials were small.

pmid:32127289.authors: Mason SA, Trewin AJ, Parker L, et al.
pmid:32127289.title: Antioxidant supplements and endurance exercise: Current evidence and mechanistic insights.
pmid:32127289.finding: Review concluding that chronic intake of 1000 mg vitamin C plus vitamin E is not recommended during heavy training, and that most marketed antioxidant compounds lack supportive human evidence.

pmid:17869589.authors: Radak Z, Chung HY, Koltai E, et al.
pmid:17869589.title: Exercise, oxidative stress and hormesis.
pmid:17869589.finding: Review framing exercise as a hormetic stressor: repeated moderate ROS exposure up-regulates antioxidant and repair systems, with a bell-shaped dose-response curve.

pmid:26893258.authors: Powers SK, Radak Z, Ji LL
pmid:26893258.title: Exercise-induced oxidative stress: past, present and future.
pmid:26893258.finding: Review of sources of exercise-induced ROS (mitochondria, NADPH oxidases, xanthine oxidase) and evidence that these ROS act as signals required for training adaptation.

pmid:27770706.title: Nrf2 mediates redox adaptations to exercise.
pmid:27770706.finding: Review of evidence that acute exercise activates Nrf2 and that repeated bouts up-regulate Nrf2-controlled antioxidant defences, with emerging human data.

pmid:40834031.authors: Torres-Rojo FI, Enríquez-Del Castillo LA, González-Chávez SA, et al.
pmid:40834031.title: Effect of exercise intensity on redox biomarkers in healthy adults: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials.
pmid:40834031.finding: Chronic exercise training raised antioxidant capacity and lowered pro-oxidant markers in healthy adults; the effect was significant for vigorous protocols but not for non-vigorous ones.

pmid:36139825.authors: Zhou Z, Chen C, Teo EC, et al.
pmid:36139825.title: Intracellular Oxidative Stress Induced by Physical Exercise in Adults: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
pmid:36139825.finding: Exercise-induced oxidative damage (8-OHdG, F2-isoprostanes, protein carbonyls) depends on intensity times volume; moderate continuous exercise and low-volume HIIT carried the lowest probability of large oxidative stress in unhealthy adults.

pmid:39914379.authors: Cordeiro LS, Linhares DG, Castro JBP, et al.
pmid:39914379.title: Impacts of Resistance Training on Endogenous Antioxidants in Older Individuals: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
pmid:39914379.finding: Resistance training in healthy older adults raised glutathione peroxidase (SMD 0.57) but did not significantly change catalase or total antioxidant activity.

pmid:20139793.authors: Campbell PT, Gross MD, Potter JD, et al.
pmid:20139793.title: Effect of exercise on oxidative stress: a 12-month randomized, controlled trial.
pmid:20139793.finding: 12 months of aerobic exercise (>=45 min/day, 5 days/week, 60-75% HRmax) lowered F2-isoprostanes 6% vs controls (not significant overall); women whose VO2max rose >15% had a 14% reduction.

pmid:33740420.authors: Flockhart M, Nilsson LC, Tais S, et al.
pmid:33740420.title: Excessive exercise training causes mitochondrial functional impairment and decreases glucose tolerance in healthy volunteers.
pmid:33740420.n: healthy volunteers (small progressive-load training study) plus elite athletes
pmid:33740420.finding: When training load was ramped up over 4 weeks, the highest-load week caused a sharp fall in intrinsic mitochondrial function and impaired glucose tolerance.

pmid:17697935.authors: Margonis K, Fatouros IG, Jamurtas AZ, et al.
pmid:17697935.title: Oxidative stress biomarkers responses to physical overtraining: implications for diagnosis.
pmid:17697935.finding: An overreaching resistance-training block raised urinary isoprostanes 7-fold, TBARS 56% and protein carbonyls 73% and lowered GSH 31%; markers tracked the performance decline.

pmid:11585710.authors: Mastaloudis A, Leonard SW, Traber MG
pmid:11585710.title: Oxidative stress in athletes during extreme endurance exercise.
pmid:11585710.finding: A 50 km ultramarathon (~6.5 h) raised plasma F2-isoprostanes from 75 to 131 pg/ml, with return to baseline by 24 h.

pmid:33239350.authors: Bull FC, Al-Ansari SS, Biddle S, et al.
pmid:33239350.title: World Health Organization 2020 guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour.
pmid:33239350.finding: WHO 2020 guidelines: adults should do 150-300 min/week of moderate or 75-150 min/week of vigorous aerobic activity, muscle strengthening on >=2 days/week, and limit sedentary time.

pmid:31721213.authors: Dirks ML, Miotto PM, Goossens GH, et al.
pmid:31721213.title: Short-term bed rest-induced insulin resistance cannot be explained by increased mitochondrial H(2) O(2) emission.
pmid:31721213.finding: Short-term bed rest cut insulin sensitivity by 42% and lowered mitochondrial respiration, but did not raise resting mitochondrial H2O2 emission or oxidative stress markers.

pmid:32502393.authors: Vaccaro A, Kaplan Dor Y, Nambara K, et al.
pmid:32502393.title: Sleep Loss Can Cause Death through Accumulation of Reactive Oxygen Species in the Gut.
pmid:32502393.finding: In flies and mice, severe sleep deprivation caused ROS accumulation in the gut; oral antioxidants or gut-targeted antioxidant enzymes prevented early death.

pmid:37717072.authors: Shah R, Shah VK, Emin M, et al.
pmid:37717072.title: Mild sleep restriction increases endothelial oxidative stress in female persons.
pmid:37717072.finding: Six weeks of sleeping 1.5 h less than habitual (randomized crossover) increased endothelial-cell oxidative stress without a compensatory antioxidant response.

pmid:28738082.authors: Trivedi MS, Holger D, Bui AT, et al.
pmid:28738082.title: Short-term sleep deprivation leads to decreased systemic redox metabolites and altered epigenetic status.
pmid:28738082.finding: One night of total sleep deprivation significantly lowered plasma glutathione, cysteine, ATP and homocysteine.

pmid:28933565.authors: Nagata C, Tamura T, Wada K, et al.
pmid:28933565.title: Sleep duration, nightshift work, and the timing of meals and urinary levels of 8-isoprostane and 6-sulfatoxymelatonin in Japanese women.
pmid:28933565.finding: Women sleeping 6 h or less had about 12% higher urinary 8-isoprostane than women sleeping more than 8 h.

pmid:26039963.authors: Watson NF, Badr MS, Belenky G, et al.
pmid:26039963.title: Recommended Amount of Sleep for a Healthy Adult: A Joint Consensus Statement of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and Sleep Research Society.
pmid:26039963.finding: AASM/SRS consensus statement: adults should sleep 7 or more hours per night on a regular basis.

pmid:28652381.authors: Bhatti P, Mirick DK, Randolph TW, et al.
pmid:28652381.title: Oxidative DNA damage during night shift work.
pmid:28652381.finding: During night work (low melatonin) urinary 8-OH-dG excretion was only 20% of that during night sleep, interpreted as reduced repair of oxidative DNA lesions.

pmid:39993913.authors: Zanif U, Lai AS, Parks J, et al.
pmid:39993913.title: Melatonin supplementation and oxidative DNA damage repair capacity among night shift workers: a randomised placebo-controlled trial.
pmid:39993913.finding: Melatonin taken before day sleep for 4 weeks gave a borderline-significant 1.8-fold increase in urinary 8-OH-dG during day sleep, suggesting improved oxidative DNA repair.

pmid:36322225.authors: Hosseini H, Homayouni-Tabrizi M, Amiri H, et al.
pmid:36322225.title: The effect of continuous positive airway pressure on total antioxidant capacity in obstructive sleep apnea: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
pmid:36322225.finding: CPAP treatment of obstructive sleep apnea increased total antioxidant capacity (SMD 0.50).

pmid:8964113.authors: Reilly M, Delanty N, Lawson JA, et al.
pmid:8964113.title: Modulation of oxidant stress in vivo in chronic cigarette smokers.
pmid:8964113.finding: Urinary 8-epi-PGF2a rose with smoking dose (heavy 177, moderate 93, nonsmokers 54 pmol/mmol) and fell within 2-3 weeks of quitting; high-dose vitamin C lowered it, vitamin E alone did not.

pmid:10944241.authors: Pilz H, Oguogho A, Chehne F, et al.
pmid:10944241.title: Quitting cigarette smoking results in a fast improvement of in vivo oxidation injury (determined via plasma, serum and urinary isoprostane).
pmid:10944241.finding: Isoprostanes in plasma, serum and urine dropped within days of quitting and reached a new steady state about 4 weeks after cessation.

pmid:27932354.authors: King CC, Piper ME, Gepner AD, et al.
pmid:27932354.title: Longitudinal Impact of Smoking and Smoking Cessation on Inflammatory Markers of Cardiovascular Disease Risk.
pmid:27932354.finding: Smoking heaviness was independently tied to urinary F2-isoprostanes; after one year, successful quitters had lower F2-isoprostanes and white-cell counts despite gaining weight.

pmid:18324566.authors: Joseph AM, Hecht SS, Murphy SE, et al.
pmid:18324566.title: Smoking reduction fails to improve clinical and biological markers of cardiac disease: a randomized controlled trial.
pmid:18324566.finding: Cutting cigarettes from ~27 to ~18/day over 6 months did not change F2-isoprostanes, inflammatory markers or symptoms; only carbon monoxide fell.

pmid:11466122.authors: Otsuka R, Watanabe H, Hirata K, et al.
pmid:11466122.title: Acute effects of passive smoking on the coronary circulation in healthy young adults.
pmid:11466122.finding: A 30-minute exposure to environmental tobacco smoke reduced coronary flow velocity reserve in healthy nonsmokers (4.4 to 3.4), indicating acute coronary endothelial dysfunction.

pmid:31429895.authors: Duncan MS, Freiberg MS, Greevy RA Jr, et al.
pmid:31429895.title: Association of Smoking Cessation With Subsequent Risk of Cardiovascular Disease.
pmid:31429895.finding: Quitting was linked to 39% lower CVD risk within 5 years versus continued smoking, but heavy smokers' risk stayed above never-smokers for well over 5 years (10-15+ years).

pmid:9644196.authors: Bermúdez E, Stone K, Carter KM, et al.
pmid:9644196.title: Environmental tobacco smoke is just as damaging to DNA as mainstream smoke.
pmid:9644196.finding: Tar from environmental (secondhand) tobacco smoke generated hydrogen peroxide and nicked DNA in cells much like mainstream-smoke tar; catalase was protective.

pmid:15911719.title: Cardiovascular effects of secondhand smoke: nearly as large as smoking.
pmid:15911719.finding: Secondhand smoke raises coronary heart disease risk ~30%; even brief exposure produces effects on platelets, endothelium and oxidative stress averaging 80-90% of those of chronic active smoking.

pmid:30356972.authors: Siti Hajar MH, Zulkefli S, Juwita S, et al.
pmid:30356972.title: Metabolic, inflammatory, and oxidative stress markers in women exposed to secondhand smoke.
pmid:30356972.finding: Women with modest secondhand-smoke exposure (>=15 min on >=2 days/week) did not differ from unexposed women in 8-isoprostane, oxidized LDL or inflammatory markers.

pmid:27108682.authors: Carnevale R, Sciarretta S, Violi F, et al.
pmid:27108682.title: Acute Impact of Tobacco vs Electronic Cigarette Smoking on Oxidative Stress and Vascular Function.
pmid:27108682.finding: A single e-cigarette and a single tobacco cigarette both acutely raised 8-iso-PGF2a and NOX2 activation and lowered flow-mediated dilation; the e-cigarette's oxidative effects were smaller.

pmid:34289969.authors: Christensen CH, Chang JT, Rostron BL, et al.
pmid:34289969.title: Biomarkers of Inflammation and Oxidative Stress among Adult Former Smoker, Current E-Cigarette Users-Results from Wave 1 PATH Study.
pmid:34289969.finding: Former smokers who now only vape had F2-isoprostane levels similar to former smokers using nothing; dual users had 9% higher levels than cigarette-only smokers.

pmid:27113031.authors: Sharma R, Harlev A, Agarwal A, et al.
pmid:27113031.title: Cigarette Smoking and Semen Quality: A New Meta-analysis Examining the Effect of the 2010 World Health Organization Laboratory Methods for the Examination of Human Semen.
pmid:27113031.finding: Smoking was associated with lower sperm count, motility and morphology, with larger effects in moderate/heavy smokers.

pmid:18078827.title: CYP2E1 and oxidative liver injury by alcohol.
pmid:18078827.finding: Review: chronic ethanol induces CYP2E1, which leaks superoxide and hydrogen peroxide and drives lipid peroxidation in alcoholic liver injury.

pmid:22859618.authors: Schrieks IC, van den Berg R, Sierksma A, et al.
pmid:22859618.title: Effect of red wine consumption on biomarkers of oxidative stress.
pmid:22859618.finding: Four weeks of 450 ml/day red wine (4 drinks, 41 g alcohol) raised urinary 8-iso-PGF2a versus the same wine dealcoholized (157 vs 141 pg/mg creatinine).

pmid:29676281.authors: Wood AM, Kaptoge S, Butterworth AS, et al.
pmid:29676281.title: Risk thresholds for alcohol consumption: combined analysis of individual-participant data for 599 912 current drinkers in 83 prospective studies.
pmid:29676281.finding: All-cause mortality was lowest at or below ~100 g alcohol per week and rose with higher intake; stroke, heart failure and fatal hypertensive disease rose roughly linearly.

pmid:17709633.authors: Pou KM, Massaro JM, Hoffmann U, et al.
pmid:17709633.title: Visceral and subcutaneous adipose tissue volumes are cross-sectionally related to markers of inflammation and oxidative stress: the Framingham Heart Study.
pmid:17709633.finding: Visceral fat was more strongly associated with urinary isoprostanes than subcutaneous abdominal fat.

pmid:27803047.authors: Duggan C, Tapsoba JD, Wang CY, et al.
pmid:27803047.title: Dietary Weight Loss, Exercise, and Oxidative Stress in Postmenopausal Women: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
pmid:27803047.finding: 12 months of calorie-restricted weight-loss diet lowered F2-isoprostanes by ~23% (diet) and ~24% (diet plus exercise) vs 3% in controls; greater weight loss gave greater reductions.

pmid:28319890.authors: Monzo-Beltran L, Vazquez-Tarragón A, Cerdà C, et al.
pmid:28319890.title: One-year follow-up of clinical, metabolic and oxidative stress profile of morbid obese patients after laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy. 8-oxo-dG as a clinical marker.
pmid:28319890.n: morbidly obese patients vs normal-weight controls
pmid:28319890.finding: Morbidly obese patients had raised urinary F2-isoprostanes and 8-oxo-dG; after sleeve gastrectomy these declined progressively and antioxidant enzymes recovered over one year.

pmid:21959342.authors: Il'yasova D, Wang F, Spasojevic I, et al.
pmid:21959342.title: Urinary F2-isoprostanes, obesity, and weight gain in the IRAS cohort.
pmid:21959342.finding: Urinary F2-isoprostanes were higher with obesity cross-sectionally, yet some isoprostanes predicted less weight gain over 5 years, cautioning against naive reading of the marker.

pmid:23242914.authors: Sermondade N, Faure C, Fezeu L, et al.
pmid:23242914.title: BMI in relation to sperm count: an updated systematic review and collaborative meta-analysis.
pmid:23242914.finding: Obesity was associated with higher odds of oligozoospermia or azoospermia (OR 1.28; morbid obesity OR 2.04).

pmid:32835677.authors: Li Z, Liu Q, Xu Z, et al.
pmid:32835677.title: Association between short-term exposure to ambient particulate air pollution and biomarkers of oxidative stress: A meta-analysis.
pmid:32835677.finding: Each 10 ug/m3 rise in short-term PM2.5 was associated with 1.6% higher malondialdehyde and a borderline 2.1% higher 8-OHdG.

pmid:28669628.title: Role of oxidative stress in cardiovascular disease outcomes following exposure to ambient air pollution.
pmid:28669628.finding: Review of epidemiological, controlled-exposure and experimental data concluding that oxidative stress is central to the cardiovascular effects of ambient air pollution.

pmid:26022815.authors: Chen R, Zhao A, Chen H, et al.
pmid:26022815.title: Cardiopulmonary benefits of reducing indoor particles of outdoor origin: a randomized, double-blind crossover trial of air purifiers.
pmid:26022815.finding: 48 h of real vs sham air purification cut indoor PM2.5 by 57% (96 to 41 ug/m3) and lowered inflammatory and thrombotic markers (e.g., myeloperoxidase -33%) and blood pressure.

pmid:33682970.authors: Wang Y, Zhao Y, Xue L, et al.
pmid:33682970.title: Effects of air purification of indoor PM(2.5) on the cardiorespiratory biomarkers in young healthy adults.
pmid:33682970.finding: One week of real vs sham HEPA purification lowered diastolic blood pressure, exhaled NO and 8-isoprostane and improved lung function.

pmid:34630006.authors: Hoffmann B, Boogaard H, de Nazelle A, et al.
pmid:34630006.title: WHO Air Quality Guidelines 2021-Aiming for Healthier Air for all: A Joint Statement by Medical, Public Health, Scientific Societies and Patient Representative Organisations.
pmid:34630006.finding: Joint statement endorsing the WHO 2021 Air Quality Guidelines, including annual mean PM2.5 not exceeding 5 ug/m3 and peak-season 8-h ozone not exceeding 60 ug/m3.

pmid:22452928.authors: Forchhammer L, Møller P, Riddervold IS, et al.
pmid:22452928.title: Controlled human wood smoke exposure: oxidative stress, inflammation and microvascular function.
pmid:22452928.finding: Three-hour controlled exposures to 220-354 ug/m3 particles from a modern wood stove had no effect on oxidatively damaged DNA, inflammatory markers or microvascular function.

pmid:17704195.authors: Barregard L, Sällsten G, Andersson L, et al.
pmid:17704195.title: Experimental exposure to wood smoke: effects on airway inflammation and oxidative stress.
pmid:17704195.finding: Four-hour exposure to 240-280 ug/m3 wood smoke raised malondialdehyde in exhaled breath condensate and alveolar NO, indicating airway oxidative stress.

pmid:23962958.authors: Lin W, Brunekreef B, Gehring U
pmid:23962958.title: Meta-analysis of the effects of indoor nitrogen dioxide and gas cooking on asthma and wheeze in children.
pmid:23962958.finding: Gas cooking was associated with higher odds of childhood asthma (OR 1.32) and indoor NO2 with current wheeze (OR 1.15 per 15 ppb).

pmid:37638371.authors: Li W, Long C, Fan T, et al.
pmid:37638371.title: Gas cooking and respiratory outcomes in children: A systematic review.
pmid:37638371.finding: Systematic review concluding the gas-cooking and childhood asthma literature is heterogeneous, mostly cross-sectional and low quality, and insufficient to establish causation.

pmid:25653189.title: Oxidation events and skin aging.
pmid:25653189.finding: Review: UV drives skin photoaging through direct DNA damage and indirect ROS/RNS-mediated oxidation of lipids, proteins and DNA.

pmid:23732711.authors: Hughes MC, Williams GM, Baker P, et al.
pmid:23732711.title: Sunscreen and prevention of skin aging: a randomized trial.
pmid:23732711.finding: Daily broad-spectrum sunscreen for 4.5 years gave 24% less skin aging than discretionary use; 30 mg/day beta-carotene had no overall effect.

pmid:17015167.authors: Hanson KM, Gratton E, Bardeen CJ
pmid:17015167.title: Sunscreen enhancement of UV-induced reactive oxygen species in the skin.
pmid:17015167.finding: Organic UV filters that penetrate into the epidermis increased UV-induced ROS above unprotected skin after about 60 minutes, arguing for reapplication.

pmid:30415629.authors: Manson JE, Cook NR, Lee IM, et al.
pmid:30415629.title: Vitamin D Supplements and Prevention of Cancer and Cardiovascular Disease.
pmid:30415629.finding: Vitamin D3 2000 IU/day for a median 5.3 years did not lower invasive cancer or major cardiovascular events (VITAL).

pmid:15574496.authors: Epel ES, Blackburn EH, Lin J, et al.
pmid:15574496.title: Accelerated telomere shortening in response to life stress.
pmid:15574496.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
pmid:15574496.finding: Higher perceived and chronic stress was associated with higher oxidative stress, lower telomerase and telomeres shorter by the equivalent of about a decade of aging.

pmid:25462890.authors: Black CN, Bot M, Scheffer PG, et al.
pmid:25462890.title: Is depression associated with increased oxidative stress? A systematic review and meta-analysis.
pmid:25462890.finding: Depression was associated with higher 8-OHdG (g = 0.31) and F2-isoprostanes (g = 0.48).

pmid:28963884.authors: Pascoe MC, Thompson DR, Ski CF
pmid:28963884.title: Yoga, mindfulness-based stress reduction and stress-related physiological measures: A meta-analysis.
pmid:28963884.finding: Yoga-based practices, versus active controls, lowered cortisol, ambulatory blood pressure and resting heart rate; trials were heterogeneous.

pmid:28670311.authors: Buric I, Farias M, Jong J, et al.
pmid:28670311.title: What Is the Molecular Signature of Mind-Body Interventions? A Systematic Review of Gene Expression Changes Induced by Meditation and Related Practices.
pmid:28670311.finding: Meditation, yoga, tai chi and related practices were associated with down-regulation of NF-kB pathway gene expression; studies were small and heterogeneous.

pmid:24280463.authors: Hegde SV, Adhikari P, Shetty S, et al.
pmid:24280463.title: Effect of community-based yoga intervention on oxidative stress and glycemic parameters in prediabetes: a randomized controlled trial.
pmid:24280463.finding: Three months of community yoga lowered malondialdehyde versus wait-list control but did not change antioxidant levels; no active control.

pmid:25705824.authors: Laukkanen T, Khan H, Zaccardi F, et al.
pmid:25705824.title: Association between sauna bathing and fatal cardiovascular and all-cause mortality events.
pmid:25705824.finding: Compared with one session/week, 4-7 sauna sessions/week was associated with 63% lower sudden cardiac death and lower CVD and all-cause mortality; sessions >19 min were also associated with lower risk.

pmid:29897261.authors: Kunutsor SK, Laukkanen T, Laukkanen JA
pmid:29897261.title: Longitudinal associations of sauna bathing with inflammation and oxidative stress: the KIHD prospective cohort study.
pmid:29897261.finding: 4-7 sauna sessions/week was associated with lower CRP and leukocyte counts over 11 years, but not with gamma-glutamyltransferase, the oxidative-stress proxy studied.

pmid:30077204.authors: Laukkanen JA, Laukkanen T, Kunutsor SK
pmid:30077204.title: Cardiovascular and Other Health Benefits of Sauna Bathing: A Review of the Evidence.
pmid:30077204.finding: Review of observational and interventional evidence linking Finnish sauna bathing to lower blood pressure, cardiovascular disease and mortality, with proposed vascular and autonomic mechanisms.

pmid:27270841.authors: Brunt VE, Howard MJ, Francisco MA, et al.
pmid:27270841.title: Passive heat therapy improves endothelial function, arterial stiffness and blood pressure in sedentary humans.
pmid:27270841.finding: Eight weeks of 40.5 C hot-water immersion 4-5 times/week (rectal temperature >=38.5 C for 60 min) doubled flow-mediated dilation (5.6 to 10.9%) and lowered blood pressure versus thermoneutral sham.

pmid:23411620.authors: Garolla A, Torino M, Sartini B, et al.
pmid:23411620.title: Seminal and molecular evidence that sauna exposure affects human spermatogenesis.
pmid:23411620.finding: Two sauna sessions/week at 80-90 C, 15 min each, for 3 months impaired sperm count, motility, chromatin condensation and mitochondrial function; fully reversed 6 months after stopping.

pmid:10396606.authors: Siems WG, Brenke R, Sommerburg O, et al.
pmid:10396606.title: Improved antioxidative protection in winter swimmers.
pmid:10396606.finding: Winter swimmers had higher baseline erythrocyte glutathione and higher SOD and catalase activity, interpreted as adaptation to repeated cold-induced oxidative stress.

pmid:36137565.authors: Esperland D, de Weerd L, Mercer JB
pmid:36137565.title: Health effects of voluntary exposure to cold water - a continuing subject of debate.
pmid:36137565.finding: Review of voluntary cold-water immersion: studies are small and heterogeneous; possible benefits on insulin sensitivity and adipose tissue, but no firm conclusions.

pmid:28833689.authors: Tipton MJ, Collier N, Massey H, et al.
pmid:28833689.title: Cold water immersion: kill or cure?
pmid:28833689.finding: Review of cold-water immersion as hazard (cold shock, drowning, cardiac arrest, hypothermia) and treatment; evidence for many claimed benefits ranges from credible to anecdotal.

pmid:26174323.authors: Roberts LA, Raastad T, Markworth JF, et al.
pmid:26174323.title: Post-exercise cold water immersion attenuates acute anabolic signalling and long-term adaptations in muscle to strength training.
pmid:26174323.finding: Ten minutes of cold-water immersion after each strength session for 12 weeks blunted gains in strength and muscle mass versus active recovery.

pmid:21414382.title: Advances in metal-induced oxidative stress and human disease.
pmid:21414382.finding: Review: redox-active metals (iron, copper, chromium) generate radicals via Fenton chemistry, while cadmium, arsenic and lead act mainly by binding thiols and depleting glutathione.

pmid:35150710.authors: Urbano T, Filippini T, Wise LA, et al.
pmid:35150710.title: Associations of urinary and dietary cadmium with urinary 8-oxo-7,8-dihydro-2'-deoxyguanosine and blood biochemical parameters.
pmid:35150710.finding: Urinary and dietary cadmium were positively and linearly correlated with urinary 8-oxodG in non-smoking blood donors.

pmid:31678726.authors: Kim SS, Meeker JD, Keil AP, et al.
pmid:31678726.title: Exposure to 17 trace metals in pregnancy and associations with urinary oxidative stress biomarkers.
pmid:31678726.finding: Among 17 urinary metals, the strongest associations with 8-isoprostane and 8-OHdG were for essential selenium and copper, illustrating confounding in spot-urine biomarker studies.

pmid:25402001.authors: Ferguson KK, McElrath TF, Chen YH, et al.
pmid:25402001.title: Urinary phthalate metabolites and biomarkers of oxidative stress in pregnant women: a repeated measures analysis.
pmid:25402001.finding: Urinary phthalate metabolites were associated with higher urinary 8-OHdG and 8-isoprostane across repeated measures in pregnancy.

pmid:37813138.authors: Chen JC, Baumert BO, Li Y, et al.
pmid:37813138.title: Associations of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, polychlorinated biphenyls, organochlorine pesticides, and polybrominated diphenyl ethers with oxidative stress markers: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
pmid:37813138.finding: Associations of PFAS, PCBs, organochlorine pesticides and PBDEs with oxidative stress markers were mostly inconsistent; only a few pooled associations (e.g., DDE with malondialdehyde) were significant.

pmid:25477703.authors: Liu Z, Liu Y, Song Y, et al.
pmid:25477703.title: Systemic oxidative stress biomarkers in chronic periodontitis: a meta-analysis.
pmid:25477703.finding: Chronic periodontitis was associated with lower serum total antioxidant capacity and higher malondialdehyde and nitric oxide.

pmid:30076616.authors: da Silva JC, Muniz FWMG, Oballe HJR, et al.
pmid:30076616.title: The effect of periodontal therapy on oxidative stress biomarkers: A systematic review.
pmid:30076616.finding: Mechanical periodontal treatment generally reduced oxidative markers (8-OHdG, total oxidant status) in saliva and gingival fluid, and in serum in most studies.

pmid:17486089.authors: Ohsawa I, Ishikawa M, Takahashi K, et al.
pmid:17486089.title: Hydrogen acts as a therapeutic antioxidant by selectively reducing cytotoxic oxygen radicals.
pmid:17486089.finding: Molecular hydrogen selectively reduced hydroxyl radical and peroxynitrite in cells and, inhaled, limited brain ischemia-reperfusion injury in rats.

pmid:34601077.authors: Zanini D, Todorovic N, Korovljev D, et al.
pmid:34601077.title: The effects of 6-month hydrogen-rich water intake on molecular and phenotypic biomarkers of aging in older adults aged 70 years and over: A randomized controlled pilot trial.
pmid:34601077.finding: Pilot trial of 0.5 L/day hydrogen-rich water for 6 months reported small differences in telomere length and some molecular markers; exploratory, many outcomes.

pmid:37259294.authors: Todorovic N, Fernández-Landa J, Santibañez A, et al.
pmid:37259294.title: The Effects of Hydrogen-Rich Water on Blood Lipid Profiles in Clinical Populations: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
pmid:37259294.finding: Hydrogen-rich water modestly lowered total cholesterol, LDL and triglycerides in small clinical trials (pooled SMD about -0.2 to -0.4).

pmid:22291721.authors: Chevalier G, Sinatra ST, Oschman JL, et al.
pmid:22291721.title: Earthing: health implications of reconnecting the human body to the Earth's surface electrons.
pmid:22291721.finding: Narrative review by proponents of earthing summarizing small studies claiming better sleep, less pain and other effects from conductive contact with the ground.

pmid:26505864.authors: Liu J, Zhang P, Tian J, et al.
pmid:26505864.title: Ozone therapy for treating foot ulcers in people with diabetes.
pmid:26505864.finding: Cochrane review: three small, high or unclear risk-of-bias trials; no firm conclusions possible on ozone therapy for diabetic foot ulcers.

pmid:1907548.authors: Aebi S, Assereto R, Lauterburg BH
pmid:1907548.title: High-dose intravenous glutathione in man. Pharmacokinetics and effects on cyst(e)ine in plasma and urine.
pmid:1907548.finding: Intravenous glutathione (2 g/m2) had a plasma half-life of about 14 minutes and was rapidly broken down or excreted in urine.

pmid:24791752.authors: Richie JP Jr, Nichenametla S, Neidig W, et al.
pmid:24791752.title: Randomized controlled trial of oral glutathione supplementation on body stores of glutathione.
pmid:24791752.finding: Oral glutathione 250-1000 mg/day for 6 months raised blood glutathione stores by 17-35%, which returned to baseline after a 1-month washout.

pmid:40500991.authors: Luk HY, Jiwan NC, Appell CR, et al.
pmid:40500991.title: Passive dehydration increases oxidative stress and mTOR signalling pathway activation in young men following resistance exercise.
pmid:40500991.finding: Fluid restriction from 24 h before resistance exercise raised muscle H2O2 compared with euhydration.

pmid:28450347.authors: Aengevaeren VL, Mosterd A, Braber TL, et al.
pmid:28450347.title: Relationship Between Lifelong Exercise Volume and Coronary Atherosclerosis in Athletes.
pmid:28450347.finding: Men with lifelong exercise volume above 2000 MET-min/week had more coronary calcification (OR 3.2) and plaque, but more benign plaque composition (fewer mixed, more calcified-only plaques).

pmid:37777289.authors: Ahmadi MN, Hamer M, Gill JMR, et al.
pmid:37777289.title: Brief bouts of device-measured intermittent lifestyle physical activity and its association with major adverse cardiovascular events and mortality in people who do not exercise: a prospective cohort study.
pmid:37777289.finding: Intermittent lifestyle activity bouts of 1-3 minutes were associated with lower mortality than bouts under 1 minute, with benefit increasing with the vigorous share of each bout.

pmid:23756332.authors: Andersen K, Farahmand B, Ahlbom A, et al.
pmid:23756332.title: Risk of arrhythmias in 52 755 long-distance cross-country skiers: a cohort study.
pmid:23756332.finding: Men completing 5+ Vasaloppet 90 km races had higher AF risk (HR 1.29) and more bradyarrhythmias than those completing one.

pmid:25844730.authors: Arem H, Moore SC, Patel A, et al.
pmid:25844730.title: Leisure time physical activity and mortality: a detailed pooled analysis of the dose-response relationship.
pmid:25844730.finding: Versus no leisure activity, mortality HR was 0.80 below the guideline minimum, 0.69 at 1-2x, 0.63 at 2-3x, 0.61 at 3-5x (plateau) and 0.69 at 10x or more: no evidence of harm at very high volumes.

pmid:34242442.title: Does exercise prevent major non-communicable diseases and premature mortality? A critical review based on results from randomized controlled trials.
pmid:34242442.finding: Critical review of RCTs (~50,000 participants): exercise has not been shown to reduce all-cause mortality or CVD in older or chronically ill adults; it prevents type 2 diabetes when combined with diet.

pmid:37555441.authors: Banach M, Lewek J, Surma S, et al.
pmid:37555441.title: The association between daily step count and all-cause and cardiovascular mortality: a meta-analysis.
pmid:37555441.finding: Each 1,000 extra steps/day was associated with 15% lower all-cause mortality, with benefit starting at about 3,900 steps/day.

pmid:40255152.authors: Berry JD, Zabad N, Kyrouac D, et al.
pmid:40255152.title: High-Volume Physical Activity and Clinical Coronary Artery Disease Outcomes: Findings From the Cooper Center Longitudinal Study.
pmid:40255152.finding: High-volume activity (3000+ MET-min/week) was linked to similar coronary event risk (MI HR 0.95) but the lowest mortality (HR 0.71); CAC predicted CAD at every activity level.

pmid:31309570.authors: Bishop DJ, Botella J, Granata C
pmid:31309570.title: CrossTalk opposing view: Exercise training volume is more important than training intensity to promote increases in mitochondrial content.
pmid:31309570.finding: CrossTalk 'opposing view' arguing training volume matters more than intensity for mitochondrial content.

pmid:35147898.authors: Buffey AJ, Herring MP, Langley CK, et al.
pmid:35147898.title: The Acute Effects of Interrupting Prolonged Sitting Time in Adults with Standing and Light-Intensity Walking on Biomarkers of Cardiometabolic Health in Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
pmid:35147898.finding: Light walking breaks lowered postprandial glucose (d -0.72) and insulin (d -0.83) versus sitting and beat standing breaks; neither changed blood pressure.

pmid:42786581.authors: Chenhuichen C, Ezzatvar Y, Zambom-Ferraresi F, et al.
pmid:42786581.title: Impact of supervised physical exercise on inflammatory and oxidative stress biomarkers in older adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
pmid:42786581.finding: Supervised exercise modestly lowered CRP and raised IL-10 in adults 65+; only 6 trials addressed redox balance, suggesting improvement, with moderate-to-high bias.

pmid:36881712.authors: De Bosscher R, Dausin C, Claus P, et al.
pmid:36881712.title: Lifelong endurance exercise and its relation with coronary atherosclerosis.
pmid:36881712.finding: Lifelong endurance athletes had more coronary plaques (OR 1.86), including non-calcified proximal plaques, than healthy non-athletes; plaque composition was not more benign.

pmid:30698608.authors: DeFina LF, Radford NB, Barlow CE, et al.
pmid:30698608.title: Association of All-Cause and Cardiovascular Mortality With High Levels of Physical Activity and Concurrent Coronary Artery Calcification.
pmid:30698608.finding: Men doing 3000+ MET-min/week had slightly more CAC of 100 or above (RR 1.11) but no higher mortality even with high CAC (HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.52-1.15).

pmid:8002116.authors: De Souza MJ, Arce JC, Pescatello LS, et al.
pmid:8002116.title: Gonadal hormones and semen quality in male runners. A volume threshold effect of endurance training.
pmid:8002116.finding: High-mileage runners (~108 km/week) had lower testosterone, sperm motility and density than moderate-mileage runners or sedentary men.

pmid:40713949.authors: Ding D, Nguyen B, Nau T, et al.
pmid:40713949.title: Daily steps and health outcomes in adults: a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis.
pmid:40713949.finding: Versus 2,000 steps/day, 7,000 steps/day was associated with 47% lower all-cause mortality and lower CVD, dementia, depression and falls; curves flattened around 5,000-7,000 steps for several outcomes.

pmid:23761134.authors: DiPietro L, Gribok A, Stevens MS, et al.
pmid:23761134.title: Three 15-min bouts of moderate postmeal walking significantly improves 24-h glycemic control in older people at risk for impaired glucose tolerance.
pmid:23761134.finding: Three 15-minute post-meal walks improved 24-h glucose as well as one 45-minute morning walk and were better for evening glucose.

pmid:35788615.authors: Dos Santos M, Ferrari G, Lee DH, et al.
pmid:35788615.title: Association of the "Weekend Warrior" and Other Leisure-time Physical Activity Patterns With All-Cause and Cause-Specific Mortality: A Nationwide Cohort Study.
pmid:35788615.finding: For the same total MVPA, weekend warriors had similar mortality to regularly active people (HR 1.08, 95% CI 0.97-1.20).

pmid:22374636.authors: Dunstan DW, Kingwell BA, Larsen R, et al.
pmid:22374636.title: Breaking up prolonged sitting reduces postprandial glucose and insulin responses.
pmid:22374636.finding: 2-minute walking breaks every 20 minutes cut post-drink glucose area by about 24-30% and insulin by about 23% versus uninterrupted sitting.

pmid:31970196.authors: Dutra MT, Martins WR, Ribeiro ALA, et al.
pmid:31970196.title: The Effects of Strength Training Combined with Vitamin C and E Supplementation on Skeletal Muscle Mass and Strength: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
pmid:31970196.finding: Vitamin C/E had no effect on strength gains and possibly attenuates hypertrophy over time.

pmid:34734783.authors: Edwards SJ, Shad BJ, Marshall RN, et al.
pmid:34734783.title: Short-term step reduction reduces citrate synthase activity without altering skeletal muscle markers of oxidative metabolism or insulin-mediated signaling in young males.
pmid:34734783.finding: Cutting steps from ~13,000 to ~1,200/day for 7 days lowered citrate synthase activity without changing insulin-signalling proteins.

pmid:27475271.authors: Ekelund U, Steene-Johannessen J, Brown WJ, et al.
pmid:27475271.title: Does physical activity attenuate, or even eliminate, the detrimental association of sitting time with mortality? A harmonised meta-analysis of data from more than 1 million men and women.
pmid:27475271.finding: About 60-75 min/day of moderate activity eliminated the extra mortality of sitting more than 8 h/day, but only attenuated the risk tied to high TV time.

pmid:31434697.authors: Ekelund U, Tarp J, Steene-Johannessen J, et al.
pmid:31434697.title: Dose-response associations between accelerometry measured physical activity and sedentary time and all cause mortality: systematic review and harmonised meta-analysis.
pmid:31434697.finding: Mortality HRs for the 2nd-4th quarters of total activity were 0.48, 0.34 and 0.27; for light activity 0.60-0.38; most-sedentary quarter HR 2.63 versus least sedentary.

pmid:31951255.authors: Elliott AD, Linz D, Mishima R, et al.
pmid:31951255.title: Association between physical activity and risk of incident arrhythmias in 402 406 individuals: evidence from the UK Biobank cohort.
pmid:31951255.finding: Physical activity was associated with lower AF risk, more clearly in women (HR 0.85 at 1500 MET-min/week), and lower ventricular arrhythmia risk.

pmid:31343601.authors: Fragala MS, Cadore EL, Dorgo S, et al.
pmid:31343601.title: Resistance Training for Older Adults: Position Statement From the National Strength and Conditioning Association.
pmid:31343601.finding: NSCA position statement: resistance training 2-3 times/week counters age-related loss of strength, muscle and function, including in frail and sarcopenic adults.

pmid:24817675.authors: Francois ME, Baldi JC, Manning PJ, et al.
pmid:24817675.title: 'Exercise snacks' before meals: a novel strategy to improve glycaemic control in individuals with insulin resistance.
pmid:24817675.finding: Six 1-minute intense incline-walking intervals before meals lowered 24-h mean glucose by 0.7 mmol/L, better than 30 minutes of continuous walking before dinner.

pmid:23380634.authors: Gaskins AJ, Mendiola J, Afeiche M, et al.
pmid:23380634.title: Physical activity and television watching in relation to semen quality in young men.
pmid:23380634.finding: Men doing 15+ h/week of moderate-to-vigorous activity had 73% higher sperm concentration than those under 5 h/week; 20+ h/week TV was linked to 44% lower concentration.

pmid:25889822.authors: Gomez-Cabrera MC, Salvador-Pascual A, Cabo H, et al.
pmid:25889822.title: Redox modulation of mitochondriogenesis in exercise. Does antioxidant supplementation blunt the benefits of exercise training?
pmid:25889822.finding: Argues exercise ROS come mainly from extramitochondrial sources (NADPH oxidase, xanthine oxidase) and that 'exercise is itself an antioxidant'; antioxidant supplements may blunt mitochondriogenesis.

pmid:36167669.authors: Gorzelitz J, Trabert B, Katki HA, et al.
pmid:36167669.title: Independent and joint associations of weightlifting and aerobic activity with all-cause, cardiovascular disease and cancer mortality in the Prostate, Lung, Colorectal and Ovarian Cancer Screening Trial.
pmid:36167669.finding: Meeting aerobic guidelines plus weightlifting 1-2 times/week was associated with 41% lower mortality versus neither, compared with 32% for aerobic alone.

pmid:29934848.authors: Granata C, Jamnick NA, Bishop DJ
pmid:29934848.title: Training-Induced Changes in Mitochondrial Content and Respiratory Function in Human Skeletal Muscle.
pmid:29934848.finding: Training volume appears critical for mitochondrial content, while relative intensity matters more for mitochondrial respiratory function.

pmid:27920258.authors: Hajizadeh Maleki B, Tartibian B, Chehrazi M
pmid:27920258.title: The effects of three different exercise modalities on markers of male reproduction in healthy subjects: a randomized controlled trial.
pmid:27920258.finding: 24 weeks of moderate continuous, high-intensity continuous or interval training lowered seminal oxidative and inflammatory markers and improved semen and sperm DNA integrity, moderate training most; the group has other retracted papers.

pmid:35022163.authors: Han M, Qie R, Shi X, et al.
pmid:35022163.title: Cardiorespiratory fitness and mortality from all causes, cardiovascular disease and cancer: dose-response meta-analysis of cohort studies.
pmid:35022163.finding: Per 1-MET higher fitness, RR 0.88 for all-cause, 0.87 for CVD and 0.93 for cancer mortality; highest versus lowest fitness RR 0.47.

pmid:31604916.authors: Henríquez-Olguin C, Knudsen JR, Raun SH, et al.
pmid:31604916.title: Cytosolic ROS production by NADPH oxidase 2 regulates muscle glucose uptake during exercise.
pmid:31604916.finding: NOX2, not mitochondria, was the main source of cytosolic ROS during moderate exercise in muscle; NOX2-deficient mice had much lower exercise-stimulated glucose uptake.

pmid:30959461.authors: Henríquez-Olguín C, Renani LB, Arab-Ceschia L, et al.
pmid:30959461.title: Adaptations to high-intensity interval training in skeletal muscle require NADPH oxidase 2.
pmid:30959461.finding: In mice lacking functional NOX2, 6 weeks of HIIT produced smaller gains in running capacity, SOD2, catalase and mitochondrial proteins.

pmid:33203106.authors: Higgins MR, Izadi A, Kaviani M
pmid:33203106.title: Antioxidants and Exercise Performance: With a Focus on Vitamin E and C Supplementation.
pmid:33203106.journal: Int J Environ Res Public Health
pmid:33203106.finding: Vitamin C and E supplements are not recommended for athletes beyond specific situations; they may block anabolic signalling; a fruit- and vegetable-rich diet is advised.

pmid:30671700.authors: Ibañez-Perez J, Santos-Zorrozua B, Lopez-Lopez E, et al.
pmid:30671700.title: An update on the implication of physical activity on semen quality: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
pmid:30671700.finding: Most data show no major effect of activity on semen; recreational activity may help concentration or motility, while elite activity may harm motility, and cycling may lower concentration.

pmid:30543812.authors: Imboden MT, Harber MP, Whaley MH, et al.
pmid:30543812.title: The Association between the Change in Directly Measured Cardiorespiratory Fitness across Time and Mortality Risk.
pmid:30543812.finding: Change in directly measured VO2peak over time was inversely related to mortality (about 11% lower per 1 mL/kg/min gained), and the later test predicted death better than the first.

pmid:31707475.authors: Islam H, Bonafiglia JT, Turnbull PC, et al.
pmid:31707475.title: The impact of acute and chronic exercise on Nrf2 expression in relation to markers of mitochondrial biogenesis in human skeletal muscle.
pmid:31707475.finding: Acute and 4-week interval exercise raised Nrf2 and downstream targets in human muscle in step with mitochondrial biogenesis markers.

pmid:34669625.authors: Islam H, Gibala MJ, Little JP
pmid:34669625.title: Exercise Snacks: A Novel Strategy to Improve Cardiometabolic Health.
pmid:34669625.finding: Defines exercise snacks as 1 minute or less of vigorous exercise several times a day and summarises small proof-of-concept trials.

pmid:39427746.title: Exercise-induced adaptations to homeostasis of reactive oxygen species in skeletal muscle.
pmid:39427746.finding: Reviews sources of superoxide and H2O2 in contracting muscle and proposes peroxiredoxins as the effectors that turn low H2O2 levels into adaptive signals.

pmid:30649897.authors: Jenkins EM, Nairn LN, Skelly LE, et al.
pmid:30649897.title: Do stair climbing exercise "snacks" improve cardiorespiratory fitness?
pmid:30649897.finding: Vigorously climbing 60 stairs 3 times a day, 3 days/week for 6 weeks modestly raised VO2peak.

pmid:29089346.authors: Kamada M, Shiroma EJ, Buring JE, et al.
pmid:29089346.title: Strength Training and All-Cause, Cardiovascular Disease, and Cancer Mortality in Older Women: A Cohort Study.
pmid:29089346.finding: Strength training showed a J-shaped association with mortality; benefit at moderate amounts, with point estimates returning to 1.0 at 146+ min/week (wide CIs).

pmid:37892564.authors: Kang J, Fardman BM, Ratamess NA, et al.
pmid:37892564.title: Efficacy of Postprandial Exercise in Mitigating Glycemic Responses in Overweight Individuals and Individuals with Obesity and Type 2 Diabetes-A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
pmid:37892564.finding: Post-meal exercise reduced glucose AUC (g -0.32) and 24-h mean glucose; bouts longer than 30 minutes worked better.

pmid:39821867.authors: Kankaanpää A, Tolvanen A, Joensuu L, et al.
pmid:39821867.title: The associations of long-term physical activity in adulthood with later biological ageing and all-cause mortality - a prospective twin study.
pmid:39821867.finding: Active classes had at most 7% lower mortality, mainly short-term; after accounting for familial factors and prevalent CVD, associations weakened, suggesting genetic confounding and reverse causation.

pmid:37462704.authors: Khurshid S, Al-Alusi MA, Churchill TW, et al.
pmid:37462704.title: Accelerometer-Derived "Weekend Warrior" Physical Activity and Incident Cardiovascular Disease.
pmid:37462704.finding: Accelerometer-defined weekend warriors and regularly active people had similarly lower risks of AF, MI, heart failure and stroke versus inactive people.

pmid:41067094.authors: Kim YS, Shin YH, Oh M, et al.
pmid:41067094.title: Association of weekend warrior physical activity pattern with health outcomes: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
pmid:41067094.finding: Weekend-warrior and regular patterns had similar associations with all-cause (RR 0.76 vs 0.71), CVD and cancer mortality compared with inactivity.

pmid:38864459.authors: Kjaergaard AD, Ellervik C, Jessen N, et al.
pmid:38864459.title: Cardiorespiratory Fitness, Body Composition, Diabetes, and Longevity: A 2-Sample Mendelian Randomization Study.
pmid:38864459.finding: Two-sample Mendelian randomization: physical activity, lean mass and lower body fat raised genetically predicted VO2max, but genetically predicted VO2max was not causally associated with longevity or diabetes.

pmid:19454641.authors: Kodama S, Saito K, Tanaka S, et al.
pmid:19454641.title: Cardiorespiratory fitness as a quantitative predictor of all-cause mortality and cardiovascular events in healthy men and women: a meta-analysis.
pmid:19454641.finding: Each 1-MET higher fitness was associated with 13% lower all-cause mortality and 15% fewer CHD/CVD events; below 7.9 METs risk rose sharply.

pmid:41612409.authors: Koemel NA, Ahmadi MN, Biswas RK, et al.
pmid:41612409.title: Vigorous intermittent lifestyle physical activity (VILPA) and mortality risk among US adults: a wearables-based national cohort study.
pmid:41612409.journal: Int J Behav Nutr Phys Act
pmid:41612409.finding: About 5 VILPA bouts/day was associated with 44% lower mortality (HR 0.56), but after excluding people with prevalent CVD or cancer the confidence intervals mostly crossed 1.

pmid:35926933.authors: Kokkinos P, Faselis C, Samuel IBH, et al.
pmid:35926933.title: Cardiorespiratory Fitness and Mortality Risk Across the Spectra of Age, Race, and Sex.
pmid:35926933.finding: Lowest mortality at about 14 METs (HR 0.24); the least fit had 4-fold higher risk than the extremely fit; no increase in risk at extreme fitness across age, sex and race.

pmid:9466636.authors: Kujala UM, Kaprio J, Sarna S, et al.
pmid:9466636.title: Relationship of leisure-time physical activity and mortality: the Finnish twin cohort.
pmid:9466636.finding: Conditioning exercisers had 43% lower mortality than sedentary people, and the association persisted within twin pairs, i.e. beyond shared genes and family background.

pmid:33492548.authors: Kunutsor SK, Seidu S, Mäkikallio TH, et al.
pmid:33492548.title: Physical activity and risk of atrial fibrillation in the general population: meta-analysis of 23 cohort studies involving about 2 million participants.
pmid:33492548.finding: Most versus least active had no overall difference in AF (RR 0.99), but risk was higher in men (RR 1.20) and lower in women (RR 0.91).

pmid:32724267.authors: Lane AR, Magallanes CA, Hackney AC
pmid:32724267.title: Reproductive Dysfunction from Exercise Training: The "Exercise-Hypogonadal Male Condition".
pmid:32724267.finding: Men chronically doing endurance training can show persistently low free and total testosterone without raised LH ('exercise-hypogonadal male condition'); spermatogenesis problems may occur in some.

pmid:38599681.authors: Lang JJ, Prince SA, Merucci K, et al.
pmid:38599681.title: Cardiorespiratory fitness is a strong and consistent predictor of morbidity and mortality among adults: an overview of meta-analyses representing over 20.9 million observations from 199 unique cohort studies.
pmid:38599681.finding: High versus low fitness was associated with HR 0.47 for all-cause mortality; each 1 MET was linked to 11-17% lower mortality; certainty very low to moderate.

pmid:25082581.authors: Lee DC, Pate RR, Lavie CJ, et al.
pmid:25082581.title: Leisure-time running reduces all-cause and cardiovascular mortality risk.
pmid:25082581.finding: Runners had 30% lower all-cause and 45% lower CVD mortality than non-runners, with similar benefit across running doses down to 5-10 min/day at slow speeds.

pmid:31141585.authors: Lee IM, Shiroma EJ, Kamada M, et al.
pmid:31141585.title: Association of Step Volume and Intensity With All-Cause Mortality in Older Women.
pmid:31141585.finding: In women averaging 72 years, about 4,400 steps/day lowered mortality versus 2,700 (HR 0.59), levelling off around 7,500 steps/day; intensity did not add after volume.

pmid:33428024.authors: Lee DH, Rezende LFM, Ferrari G, et al.
pmid:33428024.title: Physical activity and all-cause and cause-specific mortality: assessing the impact of reverse causation and measurement error in two large prospective cohorts.
pmid:33428024.finding: Single or recent activity measures overstated benefit through reverse causation (J/U-shapes appeared); cumulative-average activity with lag time showed a robust inverse dose-response up to 150 MET-h/week.

pmid:25982160.authors: Leong DP, Teo KK, Rangarajan S, et al.
pmid:25982160.title: Prognostic value of grip strength: findings from the Prospective Urban Rural Epidemiology (PURE) study.
pmid:25982160.finding: Each 5 kg lower grip strength was associated with 16% higher all-cause mortality.

pmid:42304276.authors: Li GQ, Tang SY, Luo J, et al.
pmid:42304276.title: The intervention effects of resistance exercise on sarcopenia in older adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
pmid:42304276.finding: In sarcopenia, resistance training raised grip strength by 2.95 kg, gait speed by 0.15 m/s and appendicular muscle index by 0.25 kg/m2.

pmid:30847639.authors: Little JP, Langley J, Lee M, et al.
pmid:30847639.title: Sprint exercise snacks: a novel approach to increase aerobic fitness.
pmid:30847639.finding: 3 x 20-second sprints spread through the day raised VO2peak about 4%, similar to the same sprints done in one session (~6%).

pmid:31552570.authors: Loh R, Stamatakis E, Folkerts D, et al.
pmid:31552570.title: Effects of Interrupting Prolonged Sitting with Physical Activity Breaks on Blood Glucose, Insulin and Triacylglycerol Measures: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
pmid:31552570.finding: Activity breaks in sitting moderately lowered glucose (SMD -0.54), insulin (-0.56) and triglycerides (-0.26), with larger effects at higher BMI.

pmid:27396440.authors: MacInnis MJ, Zacharewicz E, Martin BJ, et al.
pmid:27396440.title: Superior mitochondrial adaptations in human skeletal muscle after interval compared to continuous single-leg cycling matched for total work.
pmid:27396440.finding: Single-leg HIIT increased citrate synthase and mitochondrial respiration more than work-matched moderate continuous training in the other leg.

pmid:27748956.title: Physiological adaptations to interval training and the role of exercise intensity.
pmid:27748956.finding: Interval training increases VO2max more than moderate training for a given volume; sprint training matches moderate training despite less volume.

pmid:31309577.authors: MacInnis MJ, Skelly LE, Gibala MJ
pmid:31309577.title: CrossTalk proposal: Exercise training intensity is more important than volume to promote increases in human skeletal muscle mitochondrial content.
pmid:31309577.finding: CrossTalk 'proposal' arguing training intensity matters more than volume for increasing human muscle mitochondrial content.

pmid:30646252.authors: Mandsager K, Harb S, Cremer P, et al.
pmid:30646252.title: Association of Cardiorespiratory Fitness With Long-term Mortality Among Adults Undergoing Exercise Treadmill Testing.
pmid:30646252.finding: Treadmill-measured fitness was inversely related to mortality with no upper limit: elite versus low performers HR 0.20.

pmid:28544643.authors: Margaritelis NV, Theodorou AA, Paschalis V, et al.
pmid:28544643.title: Adaptations to endurance training depend on exercise-induced oxidative stress: exploiting redox interindividual variability.
pmid:28544643.finding: Men with the smallest exercise-induced oxidative stress gained least in VO2max, time trial and Wingate after 6 weeks of training, supporting a role for ROS in adaptation without any supplement.

pmid:30256898.authors: Margaritelis NV, Paschalis V, Theodorou AA, et al.
pmid:30256898.title: Antioxidants in Personalized Nutrition and Exercise.
pmid:30256898.finding: Proposes that antioxidants help only people with a measured deficiency, arguing for personalised rather than blanket supplementation.

pmid:24001718.authors: Marijon E, Tafflet M, Antero-Jacquemin J, et al.
pmid:24001718.title: Mortality of French participants in the Tour de France (1947-2012).
pmid:24001718.finding: French Tour de France riders had 41% lower mortality than the general male population (SMR 0.59), though healthy-athlete selection cannot be excluded.

pmid:33356471.authors: Martinez-Negrin G, Acton JP, Cocksedge SP, et al.
pmid:33356471.title: The effect of dietary (poly)phenols on exercise-induced physiological adaptations: A systematic review and meta-analysis of human intervention trials.
pmid:33356471.finding: (Poly)phenols did not change training gains in strength, power or VO2max; isoflavones may add lean mass while resveratrol tended to impair adaptations (SMD -0.54, NS).

pmid:28465287.authors: Merghani A, Maestrini V, Rosmini S, et al.
pmid:28465287.title: Prevalence of Subclinical Coronary Artery Disease in Masters Endurance Athletes With a Low Atherosclerotic Risk Profile.
pmid:28465287.finding: Most lifelong endurance athletes had normal CAC, but male athletes more often had CAC above 300 or plaques; plaques were mostly calcified.

pmid:26243014.authors: Milanović Z, Sporiš G, Weston M
pmid:26243014.title: Effectiveness of High-Intensity Interval Training (HIT) and Continuous Endurance Training for VO2max Improvements: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Controlled Trials.
pmid:26243014.finding: Endurance training raised VO2max by 4.9 and HIIT by 5.5 mL/kg/min versus controls; HIIT beat continuous training by a small 1.2 mL/kg/min.

pmid:25064411.authors: Mínguez-Alarcón L, Chavarro JE, Mendiola J, et al.
pmid:25064411.title: Physical activity is not related to semen quality in young healthy men.
pmid:25064411.finding: Physical activity (top quartile 9.5+ h/week) was not related to semen quality.

pmid:33348059.authors: Mishima RS, Verdicchio CV, Noubiap JJ, et al.
pmid:33348059.title: Self-reported physical activity and atrial fibrillation risk: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
pmid:33348059.finding: Meeting activity guidelines was associated with lower AF risk (HR 0.94); the benefit was uncertain above about 2000 MET-min/week.

pmid:18426850.authors: Möhlenkamp S, Lehmann N, Breuckmann F, et al.
pmid:18426850.title: Running: the risk of coronary events : Prevalence and prognostic relevance of coronary atherosclerosis in marathon runners.
pmid:18426850.finding: Conventional risk scores underestimated coronary calcification in older marathon runners; higher CAC predicted events.

pmid:39390310.authors: Mølmen KS, Almquist NW, Skattebo Ø
pmid:39390310.title: Effects of Exercise Training on Mitochondrial and Capillary Growth in Human Skeletal Muscle: A Systematic Review and Meta-Regression.
pmid:39390310.finding: After adjustment, mitochondrial content rose similarly with continuous endurance (23%), HIIT (27%) and sprint training (27%); per hour, sprint and HIIT were 2.3-3.9x more time-efficient; higher frequency gave more gain.

pmid:35228201.authors: Momma H, Kawakami R, Honda T, et al.
pmid:35228201.title: Muscle-strengthening activities are associated with lower risk and mortality in major non-communicable diseases: a systematic review and meta-analysis of cohort studies.
pmid:35228201.finding: Muscle-strengthening was associated with 10-17% lower all-cause, CVD and cancer mortality, with J-shaped curves peaking at about 30-60 min/week.

pmid:28133739.title: Refuting the myth of non-response to exercise training: 'non-responders' do respond to higher dose of training.
pmid:28133739.finding: Fitness 'non-response' fell as weekly training rose from 60 to 300 min and disappeared in all non-responders after adding two more sessions a week.

pmid:26482865.authors: Morrison D, Hughes J, Della Gatta PA, et al.
pmid:26482865.title: Vitamin C and E supplementation prevents some of the cellular adaptations to endurance-training in humans.
pmid:26482865.finding: Vitamin C plus E did not stop gains in VO2peak or mitochondrial markers but prevented some cellular adaptations (e.g. SOD2) after 4 weeks of HIIT.

pmid:26966149.authors: Morseth B, Graff-Iversen S, Jacobsen BK, et al.
pmid:26966149.title: Physical activity, resting heart rate, and atrial fibrillation: the Tromsø Study.
pmid:26966149.finding: Moderate activity was associated with 19% lower AF, while high and vigorous activity was not protective (vigorous HR 1.37, NS): a J-shaped pattern.

pmid:29411631.authors: Morseth B, Løchen ML, Ariansen I, et al.
pmid:29411631.title: The ambiguity of physical activity, exercise and atrial fibrillation.
pmid:29411631.finding: Describes a J-shaped activity-AF association and proposes different mechanisms (atrial remodelling, vagal tone) at very high training volumes.

pmid:18678768.authors: Mozaffarian D, Furberg CD, Psaty BM, et al.
pmid:18678768.title: Physical activity and incidence of atrial fibrillation in older adults: the cardiovascular health study.
pmid:18678768.finding: Leisure activity and walking were associated with up to 36% lower AF incidence in older adults.

pmid:34253538.authors: Newman W, Parry-Williams G, Wiles J, et al.
pmid:34253538.title: Risk of atrial fibrillation in athletes: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
pmid:34253538.finding: Athletes had about 2.5 times the odds of atrial fibrillation of non-athlete controls (OR 2.46), with mixed-sport and younger athletes at highest risk.

pmid:22928084.authors: Nikolaidis MG, Kerksick CM, Lamprecht M, et al.
pmid:22928084.title: Does vitamin C and E supplementation impair the favorable adaptations of regular exercise?
pmid:22928084.finding: Concludes evidence on vitamin C/E blunting adaptation is contradictory, largely because of methodological differences, but that chronic non-physiological doses cannot be recommended.

pmid:39641749.authors: Norris T, Cooper R, Garfield V, et al.
pmid:39641749.title: Unpicking Causal Relationships Between Grip Strength and Cardiorespiratory Fitness: A Bidirectional Mendelian Randomization Study.
pmid:39641749.finding: Bidirectional Mendelian randomization: greater grip strength raised cardiorespiratory fitness, but fitness did not raise grip strength.

pmid:28097313.authors: O'Donovan G, Lee IM, Hamer M, et al.
pmid:28097313.title: Association of "Weekend Warrior" and Other Leisure Time Physical Activity Patterns With Risks for All-Cause, Cardiovascular Disease, and Cancer Mortality.
pmid:28097313.finding: Weekend warriors (1-2 sessions/week) had all-cause mortality HR 0.70 versus inactive, similar to regularly active people (HR 0.65).

pmid:22677079.authors: O'Keefe JH, Patil HR, Lavie CJ, et al.
pmid:22677079.title: Potential adverse cardiovascular effects from excessive endurance exercise.
pmid:22677079.finding: Hypothesis review proposing that chronic extreme endurance training may cause atrial fibrosis, coronary calcification and arterial stiffening, while acknowledging inconsistent data and low mortality in lifelong exercisers.

pmid:35247352.authors: Paluch AE, Bajpai S, Bassett DR, et al.
pmid:35247352.title: Daily steps and all-cause mortality: a meta-analysis of 15 international cohorts.
pmid:35247352.finding: Versus the lowest quartile (~3,550 steps/day), mortality HR was 0.60, 0.55 and 0.47 at ~5,800, ~7,800 and ~10,900 steps/day; benefit levelled off at 6,000-8,000 steps (age 60+) and 8,000-10,000 (under 60). Step rate added little after accounting for volume.

pmid:25384788.authors: Paulsen G, Hamarsland H, Cumming KT, et al.
pmid:25384788.title: Vitamin C and E supplementation alters protein signalling after a strength training session, but not muscle growth during 10 weeks of training.
pmid:25384788.finding: Vitamin C/E blunted hypertrophy signalling after strength sessions and some strength gains (biceps curl) but not muscle growth over 10 weeks.

pmid:22805526.authors: Pelletier DM, Lacerte G, Goulet ED
pmid:22805526.title: Effects of quercetin supplementation on endurance performance and maximal oxygen consumption: a meta-analysis.
pmid:22805526.journal: Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab
pmid:22805526.finding: Quercetin improved endurance by 0.74% and VO2max by 1.9%, judged unlikely to be meaningful.

pmid:21827635.authors: Petersen AC, McKenna MJ, Medved I, et al.
pmid:21827635.title: Infusion with the antioxidant N-acetylcysteine attenuates early adaptive responses to exercise in human skeletal muscle.
pmid:21827635.finding: N-acetylcysteine infusion during cycling blocked exercise-induced JNK activation and blunted some adaptive gene responses in muscle.

pmid:20385254.authors: Peterson MD, Rhea MR, Sen A, et al.
pmid:20385254.title: Resistance exercise for muscular strength in older adults: a meta-analysis.
pmid:20385254.finding: Resistance training raised strength by roughly 24-33% in older adults, more with higher intensity.

pmid:18923182.title: Exercise-induced oxidative stress: cellular mechanisms and impact on muscle force production.
pmid:18923182.finding: Landmark Physiological Reviews synthesis: contracting muscle makes ROS and RNS; low levels are needed for normal force and act as signals for antioxidant, stress-protein and mitochondrial genes, while high levels cause fatigue and contractile dysfunction.

pmid:38719184.authors: Powers SK, Radak Z, Ji LL, et al.
pmid:38719184.title: Reactive oxygen species promote endurance exercise-induced adaptations in skeletal muscles.
pmid:38719184.finding: Updated review arguing redox signalling plays an important role in endurance-training adaptation, while explicitly weighing how strong the evidence is that ROS are essential.

pmid:40042073.authors: Rahmati M, Lee H, Lee H, et al.
pmid:40042073.title: Associations Between Exercise Training, Physical Activity, Sedentary Behaviour and Mortality: An Umbrella Review of Meta-Analyses.
pmid:40042073.finding: Activity, steps and combined aerobic plus resistance training were linked to lower mortality with 'suggestive' (not convincing) evidence; sedentary-behaviour links were rated weak.

pmid:27747394.authors: Reynolds AN, Mann JI, Williams S, et al.
pmid:27747394.title: Advice to walk after meals is more effective for lowering postprandial glycaemia in type 2 diabetes mellitus than advice that does not specify timing: a randomised crossover study.
pmid:27747394.finding: 10 minutes of walking after each meal lowered postprandial glucose 12% more than one daily 30-minute walk (22% after the evening meal).

pmid:28102488.title: Performance and Side Effects of Supplementation with N-Acetylcysteine: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
pmid:28102488.finding: NAC (typical 5.8 g/day) did not significantly improve performance (+0.29%); side effects rose with dose.

pmid:26455890.authors: Ross R, de Lannoy L, Stotz PJ
pmid:26455890.title: Separate Effects of Intensity and Amount of Exercise on Interindividual Cardiorespiratory Fitness Response.
pmid:26455890.finding: For a fixed amount of exercise, raising intensity from 50% to 75% of VO2peak eliminated fitness non-response; low-intensity exercise failed to raise fitness in many.

pmid:27881567.authors: Ross R, Blair SN, Arena R, et al.
pmid:27881567.title: Importance of Assessing Cardiorespiratory Fitness in Clinical Practice: A Case for Fitness as a Clinical Vital Sign: A Scientific Statement From the American Heart Association.
pmid:27881567.finding: AHA scientific statement proposing cardiorespiratory fitness as a clinical vital sign because it predicts mortality as well as or better than traditional risk factors.

pmid:32207799.authors: Saint-Maurice PF, Troiano RP, Bassett DR Jr, et al.
pmid:32207799.title: Association of Daily Step Count and Step Intensity With Mortality Among US Adults.
pmid:32207799.finding: Versus 4,000 steps/day, 8,000 steps/day had HR 0.49 and 12,000 steps/day HR 0.35 for death; step intensity was not associated after adjusting for steps.

pmid:25660917.authors: Schnohr P, O'Keefe JH, Marott JL, et al.
pmid:25660917.title: Dose of jogging and long-term mortality: the Copenhagen City Heart Study.
pmid:25660917.finding: Light joggers had the lowest mortality (HR 0.22); strenuous joggers' HR was 1.97 with a very wide CI (0.48-8.14), interpreted by the authors as a U-shaped curve.

pmid:35599175.authors: Shailendra P, Baldock KL, Li LSK, et al.
pmid:35599175.title: Resistance Training and Mortality Risk: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
pmid:35599175.finding: Any resistance training was associated with 15% lower all-cause mortality; maximum reduction 27% at about 60 min/week, diminishing at higher volumes.

pmid:38831478.authors: Shailendra P, Baldock KL, Li LSK, et al.
pmid:38831478.title: Weight training and risk of all-cause, cardiovascular disease and cancer mortality among older adults.
pmid:38831478.finding: Any weight training was associated with modestly lower mortality (HR 0.94); more time gave only marginally greater reductions; no association in people doing no aerobic exercise.

pmid:24130323.title: Recent data do not provide evidence that resveratrol causes 'mainly negative' or 'adverse' effects on exercise training in humans.
pmid:24130323.finding: Letter disputing that the Gliemann data show resveratrol is 'mainly negative' or adverse for exercise training in humans.

pmid:36482104.authors: Stamatakis E, Ahmadi MN, Gill JMR, et al.
pmid:36482104.title: Association of wearable device-measured vigorous intermittent lifestyle physical activity with mortality.
pmid:36482104.finding: Three 1-2 minute bursts of vigorous incidental activity a day were associated with 38-40% lower all-cause and cancer mortality and 48-49% lower CVD mortality.

pmid:37498576.authors: Stamatakis E, Ahmadi MN, Friedenreich CM, et al.
pmid:37498576.title: Vigorous Intermittent Lifestyle Physical Activity and Cancer Incidence Among Nonexercising Adults: The UK Biobank Accelerometry Study.
pmid:37498576.finding: Daily vigorous intermittent lifestyle activity was associated with lower cancer incidence in a near-linear way, with most bouts under 1 minute.

pmid:39467622.authors: Stamatakis E, Ahmadi M, Biswas RK, et al.
pmid:39467622.title: Device-measured vigorous intermittent lifestyle physical activity (VILPA) and major adverse cardiovascular events: evidence of sex differences.
pmid:39467622.finding: In women, a median 3.4 min/day of VILPA was associated with 45% lower major cardiovascular events (HR 0.55); associations in men were weaker and less clear.

pmid:33028588.authors: Stensvold D, Viken H, Steinshamn SL, et al.
pmid:33028588.title: Effect of exercise training for five years on all cause mortality in older adults-the Generation 100 study: randomised controlled trial.
pmid:33028588.finding: Five years of supervised exercise did not lower mortality versus guideline advice overall; HIIT showed a non-significant trend (HR 0.63 vs control, 0.51 vs moderate training).

pmid:40560504.authors: Storoschuk KL, Moran-MacDonald A, Gibala MJ, et al.
pmid:40560504.title: Much Ado About Zone 2: A Narrative Review Assessing the Efficacy of Zone 2 Training for Improving Mitochondrial Capacity and Cardiorespiratory Fitness in the General Population.
pmid:40560504.finding: Narrative review concluding current evidence does not support Zone 2 as the optimal intensity for mitochondrial or fat-oxidation capacity in the general public; higher intensities matter more at low volumes.

pmid:28382551.authors: Stunes AK, Syversen U, Berntsen S, et al.
pmid:28382551.title: High doses of vitamin C plus E reduce strength training-induced improvements in areal bone mineral density in elderly men.
pmid:28382551.finding: 1000 mg vitamin C plus 235 mg vitamin E blunted the strength-training-induced rise in hip and spine bone density.

pmid:26448856.authors: Takahashi M, Miyashita M, Park JH, et al.
pmid:26448856.title: Effects of Breaking Sitting by Standing and Acute Exercise on Postprandial Oxidative Stress.
pmid:26448856.finding: After a sitting day, postprandial d-ROMs (a crude oxidative marker) tended to rise, but not after a standing or exercise day.

pmid:39638222.authors: Tari AR, Brissach DE, Ingeström EML, et al.
pmid:39638222.title: Survival of the fittest? Peak oxygen uptake and all-cause mortality among older adults in Norway.
pmid:39638222.finding: Moderately fit older adults had 59-66% lower 5-year mortality than unfit peers, with no further reduction at higher fitness.

pmid:29691431.authors: Tikkanen E, Gustafsson S, Amar D, et al.
pmid:29691431.title: Biological Insights Into Muscular Strength: Genetic Findings in the UK Biobank.
pmid:29691431.finding: Mendelian randomization suggested higher grip strength protects against coronary heart disease (OR 0.69) and atrial fibrillation (OR 0.75).

pmid:22234399.authors: Vaamonde D, Da Silva-Grigoletto ME, García-Manso JM, et al.
pmid:22234399.title: Physically active men show better semen parameters and hormone values than sedentary men.
pmid:22234399.finding: Physically active men had better progressive motility and morphology and higher FSH, LH and testosterone than sedentary men.

pmid:42760575.authors: Wahib HR, Afroundeh R, Farzizadeh R, et al.
pmid:42760575.title: Physical activity and oxidative stress biomarkers in humans: a systematic review and quantitative meta-analysis.
pmid:42760575.finding: Physical activity lowered MDA (SMD -1.02) and raised total antioxidant status, without consistent enzyme changes; heterogeneity was very high (I2 ~95%).

pmid:24144531.authors: Weston KS, Wisløff U, Coombes JS
pmid:24144531.title: High-intensity interval training in patients with lifestyle-induced cardiometabolic disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
pmid:24144531.finding: In lifestyle-related cardiometabolic disease, HIIT raised VO2peak 3.0 mL/kg/min (about 9%) more than moderate continuous training.

pmid:28401638.authors: Wewege M, van den Berg R, Ward RE, et al.
pmid:28401638.title: The effects of high-intensity interval training vs. moderate-intensity continuous training on body composition in overweight and obese adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
pmid:28401638.finding: HIIT and moderate continuous training gave similar modest reductions in body fat in overweight adults; HIIT took less time.

pmid:21122845.authors: Wise LA, Cramer DW, Hornstein MD, et al.
pmid:21122845.title: Physical activity and semen quality among men attending an infertility clinic.
pmid:21122845.finding: Regular exercise was not associated with semen quality overall, but cycling 5+ h/week was linked to low sperm concentration (OR 1.92).

pmid:22425198.authors: Wise LA, Rothman KJ, Mikkelsen EM, et al.
pmid:22425198.title: A prospective cohort study of physical activity and time to pregnancy.
pmid:22425198.finding: Vigorous activity of 5+ h/week was associated with lower fecundability (FR 0.68) in lean women; moderate activity with slightly higher fecundability (FR 1.18).

pmid:39680487.authors: Wise LA, Wang TR, Ulrichsen SP, et al.
pmid:39680487.title: A prospective study of male physical activity and fecundability.
pmid:39680487.finding: Male vigorous, moderate or total activity was not consistently associated with couples' fecundability.

pmid:20019626.authors: Yfanti C, Akerström T, Nielsen S, et al.
pmid:20019626.title: Antioxidant supplementation does not alter endurance training adaptation.
pmid:20019626.finding: Vitamin C plus E for 12 weeks of strenuous cycling did not change gains in VO2max, power output or lactate threshold.

pmid:29794946.authors: Zou P, Wang X, Sun L, et al.
pmid:29794946.title: Semen Quality in Chinese College Students: Associations With Depression and Physical Activity in a Cross-Sectional Study.
pmid:29794946.finding: Men with low physical activity had 23% lower total sperm count.

pmid:19648152.title: On the possible origins of DNA damage in human spermatozoa
pmid:19648152.finding: Proposes the two-step hypothesis: defective chromatin remodelling (poor protamination) during spermiogenesis leaves sperm vulnerable, and oxidative stress then breaks the DNA.

pmid:19494251.authors: De Iuliis GN, Thomson LK, Mitchell LA, et al.
pmid:19494251.title: DNA damage in human spermatozoa is highly correlated with the efficiency of chromatin remodeling and the formation of 8-hydroxy-2'-deoxyguanosine, a marker of oxidative stress
pmid:19494251.finding: In human sperm, poor protamination correlated strongly with 8-OHdG formation and with DNA fragmentation (P<0.001), supporting the two-step hypothesis.

pmid:18492763.authors: Koppers AJ, De Iuliis GN, Finnie JM, et al.
pmid:18492763.title: Significance of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species in the generation of oxidative stress in spermatozoa
pmid:18492763.finding: Electron leak from mitochondrial complex I in human sperm causes midpiece lipid peroxidation and loss of motility, preventable by alpha-tocopherol in vitro.

pmid:24369131.authors: Aitken RJ, Smith TB, Jobling MS, et al.
pmid:24369131.title: Oxidative stress and male reproductive health
pmid:24369131.finding: Sperm carry only OGG1, the first enzyme of base excision repair; the oocyte must finish repairing oxidised bases before the first S-phase, and errors become mutations in every cell of the embryo.

pmid:27062870.authors: Aitken RJ, Gibb Z, Baker MA, et al.
pmid:27062870.title: Causes and consequences of oxidative stress in spermatozoa
pmid:27062870.finding: Sperm are vulnerable because their membranes are rich in polyunsaturated fatty acids and they have almost no cytoplasm for antioxidant enzymes; stressed sperm default to an apoptotic pathway with mitochondrial ROS and oxidative DNA damage.

pmid:36604857.title: DNA damage in testicular germ cells and spermatozoa. When and how is it induced? How should we measure it? What does it mean?
pmid:36604857.finding: In mature sperm, hydrogen peroxide released from the midpiece (not nucleases) penetrates the nucleus and drives DNA damage; reviews what each SDF assay actually measures.

pmid:37568254.title: Male reproductive ageing: a radical road to ruin
pmid:37568254.finding: Paternal ageing brings more sperm DNA damage, epigenetic change in the germ line and a higher mutational load in offspring.

pmid:14285045.title: KINETICS OF THE GERMINAL EPITHELIUM IN MAN
pmid:14285045.finding: Classic radiolabelling study of the kinetics of the human germinal epithelium, the source of the widely quoted ~74-day duration of spermatogenesis.

pmid:16406920.authors: Misell LM, Holochwost D, Boban D, et al.
pmid:16406920.title: A stable isotope-mass spectrometric method for measuring human spermatogenesis kinetics in vivo
pmid:16406920.finding: Deuterium labelling: newly made sperm first appeared in the ejaculate after 64 +/- 8 days (range 42-76).
